agentic-ai-q1.testing: whether you can name the one property that separates an agent from "an LLM call with tools", and treat autonomy as a dial you set deliberately.
agentic-ai-q1.trap: calling any LLM-plus-tool call an agent, or treating "agentic" as a badge of sophistication.
agentic-ai-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "The line I use is: who decides the control flow, my code or the model? In a workflow, my code fixes the path and the model fills in steps. In an agent, the model's output decides the next step: which tool to call, and when it's done, in a loop."
2 · The line that matters "So it's a dial, not a switch: a single call, a fixed chain, a router that picks a branch once, a loop with tools, and a long-horizon autonomous run. The minimum to be agentic is a model, tools, a loop, some state, and a stop condition the model influences."
3 · What it costs "Moving up the dial costs predictability. Steps, cost and latency become distributions, failure modes become open-ended, and evaluation has to judge a whole trajectory. So I pick the lowest rung that solves the problem."
4 · How I've used it "In my voice interviewer, which question comes next is plain code. Only the judgement of whether an answer has a gap worth probing is the model's."
5 · Adjacent concept "The same dial, written as permissions per class of action, is how I'd present an agent to a risk committee."
Close "Agentic means the model picks the next step; how much of that I allow is a design decision."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: the model chooses the next step
stages.html:
"The test is who owns the control flow."

Workflow:code decides the pathmodel fills in a stepcode decides the next step
Agent:model outputpicks the tool, the arguments, or stopruntime executesresult goes back to the model

Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024) draws the same line: workflows are predefined code paths; agents direct their own process.

stages.name: The line that matters
stages.html:
"Five rungs, and at each one I can say who picks the next step and who decides to stop."

Rung Example Who picks the next step Stop decided by
Single call summarise this text code code
Chain extract → validate → format code code
Router classify, then one of three branches model, once code
Tool loop answer using search and a calculator model, every step model, within caps
Autonomous "fix this bug" across many files model, long horizon model + budgets + a person

Only the last two are agentic in the strict sense. The router is the cheap middle that is often enough.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html:
"Each rung up trades a number for a distribution."

Property Workflow Agent
Steps, tokens, latency per task fixed vary per task: budgets and SLOs become distributions
Failure modes the ones in my code open-ended: wrong tool, loops, invented results
Testing per step per trajectory, across several runs
Debugging a stack trace a trace of model and tool calls

Why this matters: the cost is the reason to choose the lowest rung that works.

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.claim: rules where I can, model where I must
stages.html:
"My interviewer is a workflow with one model-judged branch, on purpose." built in the prototype.

Decision Made by Why
Which move comes next Chair: rules, about 1 ms per turn must be predictable, and can't be changed by what the candidate says
Is this answer vague enough to probe? Prober: a model call judgement that can't be written as rules

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"The dial becomes a permission table."

Action class Autonomy
Read autonomous
Reversible write autonomous, logged
Irreversible or high-value a person approves

That table is the subject of autonomy-levels.

followUps.question: Is a RAG pipeline an agent?
followUps.html:
Classic RAG, no. Agentic RAG, yes.

Who decides to retrieve Agentic?
Classic RAG code: retrieve once, then generate no
Agentic RAG the model: whether, what, and whether to re-query yes

followUps.question: "Agentic is the more advanced design, so it's better."
followUps.html:
It's more flexible and less predictable; that's a trade, not a ranking.

  • Most production value: workflows with one or two model decisions.
  • An agent is justified only when the path can't be enumerated in advance.

followUps.question: What's the minimum code for an agent?
followUps.html:
A loop of about a dozen lines; everything else is production hardening.

Loop:call the model with history + tool schemasexecute the tool it asks forappend the resultrepeat until finish or a budget trips

followUps.question: How do reasoning models change the definition?
followUps.html:
They don't change the line; they change the step count.

Changes Doesn't change
More planning inside one call, so fewer loop steps if the model's output picks actions, it's agentic

followUps.question: How would you explain it to a non-technical stakeholder?
followUps.html:
"A workflow follows our recipe; an agent writes its own recipe as it goes."

  • The second is more flexible and harder to predict.
  • So we use it only where the recipe can't be written in advance, and we cap what it's allowed to do.

dontSay: "An agent is an LLM with tools." — a single tool call inside fixed code is a workflow step.
"Agents are the future, so everything should be one." — autonomy has a predictability cost.
"It's fully autonomous." — say which actions, under which budgets and approvals.

agentic-ai-q2.testing: pragmatism. Can you say no to an agent, with a checklist, and still say when one earns its cost?
agentic-ai-q2.trap: treating "agentic" as the more sophisticated and therefore better answer.
agentic-ai-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision rule "I ask four questions. Can a senior operator draw the decision tree on a whiteboard? What does a mistake cost, and can a person gate it? Do the economics and the latency survive many model calls per task? And can I define success well enough to build an eval? If the steps can be listed, or the last three answers are bad, it's not an agent."
2 · The agent's real cost "There's arithmetic behind it. Per-step reliability compounds: ten steps at ninety-five percent each is about sixty percent end to end. On top of that, cost and latency become variable and debugging means reading trajectories."
3 · The workflow's real cost "A workflow has its own cost, which is rigidity. Every new situation needs a code change, and the long tail falls through to a default branch or a person. That's the honest case for an agent: when the long tail is the product."
4 · The tell "The tell is in the traces. If the agent takes the same path every time, the model is choosing something my code could have fixed, and I'm paying for the choice."
5 · What I'd pick "So I start with a workflow, let the model decide one branch where it's needed, and add a bounded tool loop only for the step that's truly open-ended. Coding agents are the clear case where the full loop is earned."
Close "Most things labelled agents should be workflows with one or two model decisions."

stages.name: The decision rule
stages.html:
"Each question has an answer that rules the agent out."

Question If the answer is… Then
Can the steps be enumerated? yes workflow
What does an error cost? high and irreversible, with no human gate workflow, or an agent behind hard rails
Does value per task fund many calls and the wait? no workflow
Can you define and measure success? no neither yet: build the eval first

stages.name: The agent's real cost
stages.html:
"A chain of model decisions multiplies its error rates."

task success = per-step success ^ steps
0.95 ^ 10 ≈ 0.60
0.95 ^ 20 ≈ 0.36
0.99 ^ 20 ≈ 0.82      ← a better step rate helps; fewer steps helps more

Also on the bill: non-deterministic cost and latency, and trajectory-level debugging.

stages.name: The workflow's real cost
stages.html:
"A workflow is only as good as the cases I thought of."

Workflow Agent
New situation a code change handled, if the tools allow it
Long-tail inputs fall to a default branch or a person attempted
Predictability high lower
Pick when the common paths are the product the long tail is the product

stages.name: The tell
stages.html:
"I read fifty traces and look at the paths."

Observation in the traces Verdict
The same tool sequence every time it's a workflow; hard-code the path
Two or three distinct paths a router plus fixed branches
Paths differ and depend on what was observed the agent is earning its cost

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: workflow first, earn autonomy per step
stages.html:
"Autonomy is added one step at a time, each with a measurement."

Path:fixed workflowmodel decides one branchbounded tool loop for the open-ended stepmeasurewiden only if it pays

The positive case mirrors the checklist: open-ended inputs, verifiable outcomes, errors that are tolerable or gated, and enough value per task to fund the loop.

Fix layer: orchestration: this is a choice about who owns the control flow.

followUps.question: Give me an example where an agent is clearly right.
followUps.html:
Fixing a failing test in an unfamiliar codebase.

Checklist item Coding task
Path enumerable? no
Outcome verifiable? yes: the tests pass
Errors reversible? yes: version control
Value funds many calls? yes

followUps.question: "A better model will make the agent reliable enough."
followUps.html:
It raises the per-step rate; the multiplication stays.

10 steps: 0.95 → 0.60      0.99 → 0.90
 5 steps: 0.95 → 0.77      ← halving the steps at the old rate

Shorter trajectories and a check after each step move the number as much as a model upgrade.

followUps.question: 🧪 A loan-approval flow with 6 fixed checks: agent or workflow?
followUps.html:
Workflow.

  • Enumerable: six known checks.
  • Costly and regulated: an auditor needs the same path every time.
  • Model's place: inside a step, extracting fields or summarising a document.

followUps.question: How do you push back when leadership wants "an agent"?
followUps.html:
Reframe around the outcome they want.

Show Why
The workflow version reaching the same goal lower cost and variance
The one step where model judgement adds value that's where the "agent" lives

dontSay: "Agents are always the more advanced option." — advanced isn't the criterion; fit is.
A per-step accuracy with no multiplication across steps. — the task rate is what users see.
"We'll make it an agent and add guardrails later." — the rails decide if autonomy is grantable at all.

agentic-ai-q3.testing: the mechanics (what goes into context each turn, who executes the tool) and whether you design termination and budgets from the start.
agentic-ai-q3.trap: describing the happy path with no stop condition, no budget, and no mention that observations are untrusted.
agentic-ai-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "It's a loop of three beats: the model reasons about what to do, emits a structured action, and my runtime executes it and appends the result as an observation. Then the whole history goes back to the model, until it calls a finish action or a budget stops it."
2 · How it works "The model never runs anything. It only asks, with a tool name and JSON arguments. My runtime validates the call against an allow-list, executes it, and returns the result as data."
3 · Prove it "I can write it in about fourteen lines, and the important lines are the exits: a step cap, a token budget and a wall-clock deadline. At any limit I return the partial result and the reason, never a silent empty answer."
4 · What it costs or breaks "Two costs. Each turn re-sends the growing history, so tokens grow faster than the step count. And the classic failures are looping on the same failing call, and calling a tool that doesn't exist or reporting a success that never happened. Observations can also carry instructions, so they're untrusted."
5 · So what for the system "So I design the exits first: finish, caps, deadline, loop detection and a human gate. The loop body is the easy part."
Close "The loop is three beats; the engineering is in how it stops."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Reason, act, observe, repeat: the ReAct shape."

One turn:history + tool schemasmodel reasonsemits a tool callruntime executesobservation appendednext turn

ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves reasoning and acting so each decision is grounded in the last observation.

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: the runtime executes; the model asks
stages.html:
"Every arrow out of the model passes through my code."

The trust boundary is the runtime box: whatever a tool or a web page returns is text in the prompt, and can contain instructions.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
"The exits take more lines than the loop." Run with Python 3.12.

import time
def run(model, tools, max_steps=8, max_tokens=20_000, deadline_s=30.0):
    history, tokens, start = [], 0, time.monotonic()
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        if tokens > max_tokens or time.monotonic() - start > deadline_s:
            return {"status": "budget", "steps": step - 1, "partial": history}
        call, used = model(history)                  # ("tool", args) or ("finish", answer)
        tokens += used
        if call[0] == "finish":
            return {"status": "done", "steps": step, "answer": call[1]}
        result = tools[call[0]](**call[1]) if call[0] in tools else f"unknown tool {call[0]}"
        history.append((call, result))               # observation re-enters context
    return {"status": "max_steps", "steps": max_steps, "partial": history}
script = iter([(("search", {"q": "refund policy"}), 900), (("finish", "30 days"), 300)])
print(run(lambda h: next(script), {"search": lambda q: "policy: 30 days"}))
# → {'status': 'done', 'steps': 2, 'answer': '30 days'}
print(run(lambda h: (("search", {"q": "x"}), 900), {"search": lambda q: "no result"})["status"])
# → max_steps

The second run is a model that never finishes. The cap stops it; a sentence in the prompt wouldn't.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
"Cost grows with the square of the steps, and the failures are few and known."

tokens for step i ≈ base prompt + history added by steps 1 … i−1 + output
total over n steps ≈ n × base + added × n(n−1)/2 + n × output      ← the middle term is quadratic
Problem Why Control
Tokens grow faster than steps full history re-sent each turn compaction, caps, prefix caching
Looping nothing in context forces a new strategy repeated-call detection
Invented tools or results grounding weakens as context fills schema validation, allow-list
Injected instructions observations are text in the prompt treat as data; least privilege

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
"Five exits, each owned by code."

Exit Returns
finish tool the answer
Step, token or cost cap partial result + which limit
Wall-clock deadline partial result + "timed out"
Loop detected partial result + the repeated call
Human gate a pending approval, resumable

My interviewer gives every run an explicit call and token budget; on a breach a fixed closing line plays and feedback is still produced.

Fix layer: orchestration: budgets and exits live in the runtime, never in the prompt.

followUps.question: Who actually executes the tool?
followUps.html:
My runtime. The model only emits a structured request.

Round trip:model emits name + JSON argumentsruntime validatesruntime executesresult returned as a new message

followUps.question: "Tell the model in the prompt to stop when done."
followUps.html:
That's a hope, not a stop condition.

In the prompt In code
"Stop when you're done" a finish tool
"Don't repeat yourself" repeated-call detection
"Be efficient" step, token and time caps

followUps.question: 🧪 Each step adds 800 tokens of history to a 3,000-token prompt, with 300 output tokens. What do 10 steps cost?
followUps.html:
About 69,000 tokens, against 24,500 for 5 steps.

10 steps: 10 × 3,000 + 800 × 45 + 10 × 300 = 69,000
 5 steps:  5 × 3,000 + 800 × 10 +  5 × 300 = 24,500     ← doubling the steps nearly triples the tokens

followUps.question: What changes with reasoning models?
followUps.html:
The written "thought" matters less; the act-and-observe grounding stays.

  • Less needed: explicit reasoning scaffolds in the prompt.
  • Still needed: tool calls, observations, budgets and exits.

followUps.question: What would you build first in production?
followUps.html:
Budgets, step-level tracing and checkpointing, before any prompt tuning.

Without Consequence
Budgets an unbounded bill
Traces a non-deterministic loop nobody can debug
Checkpoints a restart loses the run

dontSay: A loop with no stop condition beyond "the model decides". — code owns the exits.
"The tool output is trusted because it's our tool." — it can carry text from anywhere.
"The agent calls the API." — the runtime does; the model asks.

agentic-ai-q4.testing: whether you see the model as one swappable component and the scaffolding as the engineering.
agentic-ai-q4.trap: answering "a good prompt and some tools".
agentic-ai-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "About six boxes, and the model is the least interesting one. Tools, which are typed, permissioned capabilities. State and memory. Orchestration: the loop, retries and checkpoints. Guardrails. Observability. And two things that cut across all of them: identity, meaning whose permissions the agent acts under, and budgets enforced in the runtime."
2 · The line that matters "I justify each box by the failure it prevents. No guardrails means injection reaches tools. No checkpointing means a crash loses the run. No traces means 'it did something weird' tickets nobody can debug."
3 · What it costs "That scaffolding is most of the code and most of the production failures. The model call is a few lines."
4 · How I've used it "My interviewer has the same boxes: circuit breakers around every dependency, checkpoints keyed by turn, per-run budgets, flags on input, a trace per session, and the candidate's identity bound into a signed token."
5 · Adjacent concept "Drawn as services with a queue, workers and a state store, the same boxes are the production reference architecture. The current name for all of it is the harness."
Close "The model is swappable. The durable assets are the tool contracts, the state schema and the eval set."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"The model is the policy; everything else is what lets it act safely."

Box What it is
Model picks the next action
Tools typed, permissioned capabilities
State and memory working context, checkpointed run state, long-term stores
Orchestration the loop, control flow, retries, checkpoints
Guardrails input and output validation, permissions
Observability a trace of every model and tool call
Across all: identity and budgets whose rights it acts with; caps enforced in the runtime

stages.name: The line that matters
stages.html:
"If I can't name the failure a component prevents, it doesn't belong in the diagram."

Box Without it
Typed, permissioned tools malformed calls, over-broad actions
Checkpointed state a crash loses the run; side effects half-applied
Orchestration with budgets runaway loops and bills
Guardrails injected text reaches tools with side effects
Tracing non-deterministic failures can't be debugged
Identity and authorisation the agent acts with more rights than the user

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: the scaffolding is most of the work
stages.html:
"A demo is the model box. A product is the other six."

Demo Production
Model call most of the code a few lines
Everything around it absent most of the code, and most of the incidents

Each box is also a thing to operate: a store to run, a policy to maintain, a trace bill to pay.

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.claim: the same boxes in my interviewer
stages.html:
"Each box maps to something I built." built in the prototype.

Box In the voice interviewer
Tools and model calls behind a circuit breaker per dependency
State LangGraph checkpoints, writes keyed by turn
Orchestration and budgets per-run call and token budgets
Guardrails Sentinel flags on input; it flags and never acts
Observability a trace per session
Identity the candidate's identity bound in the signed room token

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"The boxes are the harness; drawn as services, they're the reference architecture."

As services:gatewayqueueagent workerstool layer with permissionsstate storetraces
Asset Survives a model change?
Tool contracts against systems of record yes
State schema yes
Eval set and traces yes
Prompts tuned to one model re-tuned

The service view is in production-agentic-system; the harness framing in harness-or-model.

followUps.question: Which box would you build first?
followUps.html:
Tracing and budgets.

  • Tracing makes every other problem visible.
  • Budgets make every other problem bounded.

followUps.question: "The framework gives me all of that."
followUps.html:
It gives the plumbing, not the policy.

From a framework Still yours
Checkpoints, streaming, graph execution tool contracts and permissions
Retry helpers budgets and what happens at the limit
Tracing hooks the eval set and what counts as correct

followUps.question: 🧪 The agent runs under a shared service account, and a junior user asks it for payroll data. What happens?
followUps.html:
It returns the data, because the tool only sees the service account. Identity has to live in the tool layer, on every call.

Call path:user request with identityagenttool call carries the user's identityauthorised against that user's entitlements

A shared service account means the agent can do more than the person it's acting for.

followUps.question: What's the durable asset if models keep changing?
followUps.html:
Tool contracts, the eval set and the traces.

Asset Why it lasts
Tool contracts they encode your systems, not a model
Eval set it tells you whether the next model is better for you
Traces they're where new eval cases come from

dontSay: "A good prompt is most of it." — the prompt is one input to one box.
A diagram with no identity, budgets or tracing. — those are the first questions in a review.
"The framework handles production concerns." — it handles plumbing.

agentic-ai-q5.testing: whether you trade adaptivity against cost and latency, and pick by how predictable the environment is.
agentic-ai-q5.trap: naming the three patterns without the trade-off, or picking by fashion.
agentic-ai-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision rule "The axis is adaptivity against cost, and what picks the point on it is how predictable the environment is. If each observation changes what to do next, interleave. If the steps are knowable up front, plan first."
2 · ReAct's real cost "ReAct decides one step at a time with every observation in front of it. That's the most adaptive option, and it costs a large-model call per step, with the history growing each time. Early short-sighted choices can also wander."
3 · Planning's real cost "Plan-and-Execute drafts the whole plan, then runs the steps with a cheaper model or plain code. ReWOO goes further: it plans with placeholders, runs all the tool calls with no reasoning in between, then makes one synthesis call. Both save large calls. Their cost is brittleness: the plan goes stale when the world surprises it, and ReWOO can't react at all mid-run."
4 · The tell "I read the traces. If plans are thrown away after the first step most of the time, planning is wasted. If ReAct runs follow the same path every time, a plan or a workflow would be cheaper."
5 · What I'd pick "In production it's usually a hybrid: plan, execute each step with a small loop, and re-plan when a step diverges."
Close "The pattern matters less than the quality of the decomposition."

stages.name: The decision rule
stages.html:
"One question picks the pattern."

Environment Pattern
Observations change what to do next ReAct
Steps knowable up front; the model is expensive Plan-and-Execute
Steps independent; results need no interpretation between them ReWOO
Mostly predictable, with surprises plan + a small loop per step + re-plan on divergence

Sources: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022), ReWOO (Xu et al., 2023).

stages.name: ReAct's real cost
stages.html:
"Count the large-model calls for the same six-tool task."

ReAct             6 tool steps × 1 reasoning call + 1 final   = 7 big calls, history grows each time
Plan-and-Execute  1 plan + 6 cheap or code executions + 1 final = 2 big calls (+ re-plans)
ReWOO             1 plan + 6 tool calls in parallel + 1 solve   = 2 big calls, no reasoning in between
                                                                 (illustrative)
ReAct:thinkcallobservethinkcallobserve…answer

stages.name: Planning's real cost
stages.html:
"A plan is written against an imagined environment."

Plan-and-Execute:plan all stepsexecute step 1execute step 2re-plan
ReWOO:plan with placeholdersrun every tool callone synthesis call
ReAct Plan-and-Execute ReWOO
Adaptivity highest on re-plan none mid-run
Big-model calls one per step few two
Parallel tool calls no sometimes yes
Fails when it wanders the plan goes stale a result needs interpreting

stages.name: The tell
stages.html:
"The traces say which pattern I should have used."

Observation in the traces Verdict
Plans discarded after step 1, most of the time planning is wasted; interleave
ReAct runs take the same path every time a plan, or a fixed workflow, is cheaper
Re-plans cluster on one step that step needs a better tool or a check

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: a hybrid, and a better decomposition
stages.html:
"Plan for coherence, loop for adaptivity, re-plan on evidence."

Hybrid:planper step: a small bounded loopcheck the step's success criterionre-plan

A bad decomposition dooms all three equally. So the real investment is task-shaped tools and a success criterion per step. Reasoning-class models move some planning inside one call, which blurs the line without removing the trade-off.

Fix layer: orchestration.

followUps.question: Why can ReWOO parallelise and ReAct can't?
followUps.html:
ReWOO names every call up front; ReAct only knows its next call after reading the last result.

Knows all calls before running? Parallel
ReWOO yes, with placeholders yes, for independent calls
ReAct no no

followUps.question: "Reasoning models make planning patterns obsolete."
followUps.html:
They absorb some planning; they don't remove round trips.

  • Still true: cost and latency scale with tool round trips.
  • So: plan-then-execute still saves calls when steps are predictable.

followUps.question: 🧪 A plan's step 3 depends on parsing step 2's result. ReWOO?
followUps.html:
Only if step 3's input is a direct substitution.

Step 3 needs Pattern
Step 2's output pasted in as is ReWOO works
An interpretation of step 2's output Plan-and-Execute with a reasoning step between

followUps.question: How would you decide with data?
followUps.html:
Run both on the eval set and compare more than success.

Pattern Task success Big-model calls Cost per task p95 latency Re-plan rate
ReAct measure measure measure measure —
Plan + execute measure measure measure measure measure

dontSay: The three names with no cost or adaptivity trade-off. — the trade-off is the answer.
"ReAct is always best because it's adaptive." — adaptivity is paid for per step.
"We use Plan-and-Execute." — say what happens when a step diverges.

agentic-ai-q6.testing: whether you design tools for a consumer that reads literally, holds little in mind, and will do anything the tool permits.
agentic-ai-q6.trap: auto-generating one tool per REST endpoint.
agentic-ai-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I start with three questions per tool: which user intention does it serve, who's allowed to trigger it, and is it a read, a reversible write, or irreversible?"
2 · Constraints and numbers "The constraint is context. Every tool schema sits in the prompt on every turn, and selection gets worse as tools multiply. So I want the fewest tools that cover the intentions."
3 · Baseline design "The baseline has three rules. Task-shaped, not endpoint-shaped: one book-meeting tool in place of the five API calls behind it, because every step the model has to compose is a chance to fail. Few, distinct, well-named tools whose descriptions say when to use them and when not to. And inputs constrained by structure: enums over free strings, few required parameters, sane defaults."
4 · Deep-dive "Outputs and errors are prompts too. I return the few fields that matter and say when there's more. And an error tells the model what to change, not a stack trace."
5 · Failure modes "It fails through overlap between tools, danger hidden behind a flag, and a tool that can do more than its intention needs. So destructive operations are separate tools, because permissions, approvals and audit all hang off tool identity."
6 · Evolve "Then I measure tool selection on the eval set and improve it like any metric."
Close "A tool is an API designed for a reader that takes everything literally."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: the intention, the caller, the blast radius
stages.html:
"Three answers per tool, before any schema."

Question Sets
Which user intention does it serve? the tool's name and scope
Who may trigger it? the authorisation check inside the tool
Read, reversible write, or irreversible? autonomy level and whether a person approves

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Tools aren't free to add."

tool cost per turn = schemas × tokens per schema                (illustrative)
30 tools × 150 tokens  =  4,500 tokens on every turn
200 tools × 150 tokens = 30,000 tokens on every turn     ← before the task has started
More tools Effect
Longer prefix cost and latency on every turn, softened by caching
Similar descriptions selection accuracy falls

Budget: one tool call is one extra model round trip plus the tool's own latency, so a task-shaped tool that replaces four calls also removes three round trips.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"The same capability, designed twice."

❌ endpoint-shaped (the model must sequence 4 calls and guess formats)
   get_order(id) · get_payment(order_id) · post_refund(payment_id, cents, reason_code:str) · post_note(...)

✅ task-shaped (one call, constrained)
   issue_refund(order_id: str,
                amount: number ≤ order_total,
                reason: enum["damaged", "late", "wrong_item"])
   description: "Refund a delivered order. Use only after the customer confirms the amount.
                 Do NOT use for cancellations (use cancel_order)."
   returns: {"refund_id", "status", "amount"}     errors: "amount 120 exceeds order total 80"
Rule Why
Task-shaped composition happens once, in code
Description says when and when not it's the text the model chooses from
Enums, required-minimal, defaults whole classes of malformed calls can't happen

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: outputs and errors are prompts too
stages.html:
"Whatever the tool returns becomes the model's next input."

Weak Strong
Output 50 KB of raw JSON the decision-relevant fields, with "12 more available"
Error a traceback date must be YYYY-MM-DD, got 03/04
Truncation silent stated, with how to get the rest

The model can correct itself from the strong error on the next step. It can't from a traceback.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Four failures, each fixed in the tool, not in the prompt."

Failure Cause Fix
Coin-flip choices overlapping tools (search_docs vs query_kb) merge, or sharpen each description
A destructive call slips through danger as a flag on a benign tool a separate, gated tool
Malformed arguments free-text parameters enums, required fields, validation
Over-reach the tool can do more than the intention least privilege per tool
Requirement In the description Enforced outside
Refund within the order total stated the tool rejects it
Only for this user's orders — authorisation on the caller's identity
Refunds above a limit need approval stated a human gate keyed on tool name and amount

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"Selection accuracy is a number I can move."

Eval case Expected tool Chosen Arguments valid
A refund request issue_refund measure measure
A cancellation cancel_order measure measure
No tool needed none measure —
Loop:log expected against chosenconfusion pairsfix descriptions or mergere-run

Evaluation hook: selection accuracy and argument-validity rate, per release. Fix layer: tool contract.

followUps.question: Why not expose the REST API directly?
followUps.html:
Because the model would have to do the composition, and each step multiplies the error rate.

Exposed API:model sequences 4 callscarries ids and formats between them4 chances to fail
Wrapped:one tool callcode does the sequence

followUps.question: "More tools give the agent more capability."
followUps.html:
More tools give it more ways to be wrong and more context to read.

Count goes up What actually grows
Choices confusion between similar tools
Prefix tokens on every turn
Capability only if a new intention is covered

followUps.question: 🧪 The model keeps passing "tomorrow" to a date parameter. Fix?
followUps.html:
Fix it in the tool, in one of three ways.

  • Tighten the schema: format: date.
  • Make the error actionable: "use YYYY-MM-DD; today is 2026-10-01".
  • Or accept relative dates and resolve them in the tool.

followUps.question: Who owns tool contracts in an organisation?
followUps.html:
The team that owns the system of record.

Practice Why
Versioned like an API agents are consumers
Contract tests independent of any model the contract outlives the model
An owner per tool someone answers for its blast radius

dontSay: "We generate tools from the OpenAPI spec." — that's endpoint-shaped by construction.
A destructive action as a boolean parameter. — permissions and audit hang off tool identity.
"The description tells it not to." — the tool should refuse.

agentic-ai-q7.testing: that you treat this as a choice-set and context problem, not a prompt problem.
agentic-ai-q7.trap: improving the system prompt instead of reducing what the model sees per turn.
agentic-ai-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Symptom "The model calls a near-miss tool, ignores the right one, or invents one, and it's worse where names are similar."
2 · Hypotheses "My hypotheses are the size of the choice set, overlap between tools, vague descriptions, and position effects in a very long tool list."
3 · Evidence "For each eval case I know the expected tool, so I measure selection accuracy, look at which pairs get confused, and see how accuracy changes as I expose fewer tools."
4 · Root cause "Two hundred tools almost always means the tools mirror an API surface, not user intentions. And two hundred schemas in the prompt is a context problem before it's an accuracy problem."
5 · Fix "So I shrink the choice set per turn, three ways, usually combined. Consolidate into task-shaped tools, which often gets two hundred down to about thirty. Retrieve tools like documents: index the descriptions and expose only the few relevant to this step. And route by domain, so a billing agent sees only billing tools."
6 · Prevent "Then a tool registry: each new tool needs a distinct description, an owner and eval cases, and selection accuracy is tracked per release."
Close "Fixed means selection accuracy is a number that went up, with fewer tools in the window."

stages.name: Symptom
stages.html:
"Three shapes of bad selection."

Shape Example
Near miss update_order when it should be cancel_order
Ignored answers from memory when a lookup tool exists
Invented calls a tool that isn't in the list

stages.name: Hypotheses
stages.html:
"Four causes, all about what's in the window."

Hypothesis Check
Too many schemas per turn accuracy against the number of tools exposed
Overlapping tools a confusion matrix by tool
Vague descriptions do they say when not to use the tool?
Position in a long list accuracy by the tool's position

stages.name: Evidence
stages.claim: selection accuracy, by tool and by count
stages.html:
"The eval set already has the expected tool for each case."

Observation Likely cause Next action
Errors concentrate in a few pairs overlap merge the pair, or cross-reference them by name
Accuracy rises sharply with fewer tools exposed choice-set size retrieve or route
Right tool, wrong arguments weak schemas types, enums, examples
Errors spread evenly the list as a whole is too long consolidate

stages.name: Root cause
stages.html:
"The count is a symptom of how the tools were made."

How it happens:an API with 200 endpointsone tool generated per endpoint200 schemas in every promptsimilar tools blur together

Model or harness? Harness. A person handed 200 near-identical function signatures and no guidance would also pick badly.

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
"Retrieval over tool descriptions is RAG where the documents are capabilities." Toy keyword scorer; run with Python 3.12.

import re
TOOLS = {"issue_refund": "refund money for a delivered order to the customer",
         "track_shipment": "where is my order shipment delivery status tracking",
         "update_address": "change the delivery address on an order before shipping",
         "cancel_order": "cancel an order that has not shipped yet"}
words = lambda s: set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", s.lower()))
def top_k(query, k=2):
    q = words(query)
    return sorted(TOOLS, key=lambda t: -len(q & words(TOOLS[t] + " " + t.replace("_", " "))))[:k]
print(top_k("my order hasn't arrived, where is the delivery?"))   # → ['track_shipment', 'update_address']
print(top_k("I want my money back, the order was damaged"))      # → ['issue_refund', 'track_shipment']

Production replaces the keyword overlap with embeddings or a learned ranker; the shape is the same.

Approach Model sees per turn Cost
Consolidate about 30 task-shaped tools design work, once
Retrieve top-k 5–10 relevant tools a retrieval step; recall of the right tool matters
Route by domain one domain's handful an extra hop; router errors

stages.name: Prevent
stages.claim: a registry with owners and evals
stages.html:
"A new tool has to earn its place in the window."

Admission:distinct descriptionnamed ownereval cases with the expected toolselection accuracy doesn't falladmitted
Tracked per release Why
Selection accuracy the headline metric
Recall@k of the expected tool (if retrieving) a missed tool can't be chosen
Tools exposed per turn the thing I'm keeping small

Fix layer: tool contract and context assembly; the model is unchanged.

followUps.question: What if retrieval misses the right tool?
followUps.html:
Then the model can't pick it, so I measure and hedge.

  • Measure recall@k of the expected tool.
  • Keep a small always-on core set.
  • Offer a "show me more tools" action as a fallback.

followUps.question: "Better instructions in the system prompt will fix it."
followUps.html:
The problem is what's in the window; instructions add to it.

Wrong order:bad selectionmore instructionsa longer prompt, same 200 choices
Right order:bad selectionconfusion matrixfewer, sharper tools per turn

followUps.question: 🧪 Two tools have near-identical descriptions. What happens?
followUps.html:
Selection between them is close to a coin flip.

Fix When
Merge them they serve one intention
State when not to use each, naming the other they serve two

followUps.question: How does MCP change this?
followUps.html:
It makes adding tools easy, so the count problem gets worse.

With many servers connected Practice
Every server's tools loaded filter and expose per task
Third-party descriptions review and pin them; they steer the model

Protocol detail is in MCP-CONTEXT-ENGINEERING.

dontSay: "Use a bigger model." — the window is still overloaded.
A fix with no measurement of selection accuracy. — it's the one number that says it worked.
"We added a rule to the prompt for each mix-up." — that's more tokens competing with the tools.

agentic-ai-q8.testing: classification of failures, idempotency for side effects, and bounded retries.
agentic-ai-q8.trap: retrying a non-idempotent tool and double-charging someone.
agentic-ai-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Symptom "A tool returns an error, times out, or returns something malformed that the model might read as success."
2 · Hypotheses "First I classify it. Transient, like a timeout or a 503: the runtime retries with backoff and the model isn't involved. Invalid arguments: the validation error goes back to the model as an observation it can fix. Permanent, like not found or forbidden: surface it and don't loop."
3 · Evidence "In the traces I look at error rates per tool and per class. A rising invalid-argument rate points at a schema or description problem, not at the network."
4 · Root cause "The deeper issue is that side effects aren't transactional. After a timeout I don't know if the action happened, so a retry may repeat something that succeeded."
5 · Fix "So retries get two guards. Caps per tool and per run, so one failing tool can't eat the budget. And an idempotency key on anything with side effects, derived from the run and the step, so a retry or a resumed run returns the original result."
6 · Prevent "To prevent it spreading, each dependency sits behind a circuit breaker, and the final answer says what failed. A failure never quietly becomes 'I couldn't find anything'."
Close "Fixed means a retry is safe, a dead dependency fails fast, and the user is told what's missing."

stages.name: Symptom
stages.claim: an error observation in the loop
stages.html:
"Three things can come back, and the third is the dangerous one."

Returned Risk
An explicit error the model may loop on it
A timeout unknown whether the action happened
Malformed or empty output read as "no results", reported as fact

stages.name: Hypotheses
stages.html:
"The class decides who handles it."

Class Example Who handles it
Transient timeout, 429, 503 runtime: retry with backoff; no tokens spent
Invalid arguments schema or business-rule violation model: fix the call from the error
Permanent 404, 403, unsupported nobody retries; report

stages.name: Evidence
stages.claim: error rate by tool and class
stages.html:
"The mix of classes tells me where the problem lives."

Observation Likely cause Next action
Transient errors spike on one tool the dependency is unhealthy breaker opens; fallback path
Invalid-argument rate climbs after a release a schema or description change fix the tool contract
Same failing call repeated in a run the error message isn't actionable rewrite the error; loop detection
"No results" answers with tool errors in the trace failures swallowed propagate failure into the answer

stages.name: Root cause
stages.html:
"A timeout tells me nothing about what happened on the other side."

Unsafe:charge sentretrycharged twice
Safe:charge sent with a keyretry with the same keyoriginal receipt returned

The retry can come from three places: the model, the runtime, or a resumed run after a crash. Only idempotency covers all three.

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
"An idempotency key makes a replay return the first result." Run with Python 3.12.

charges, seen = [], {}
def charge(order_id, amount, idem_key):
    if idem_key in seen:
        return seen[idem_key]                    # replay → same result, no second charge
    receipt = f"ch_{len(charges) + 1:04d}"
    charges.append((order_id, amount)); seen[idem_key] = receipt
    return receipt
key = "refund:o-42:step-1"                       # derived from run + step, not random per call
print(charge("o-42", 30, key), charge("o-42", 30, key), len(charges))   # → ch_0001 ch_0001 1
Guard Rule
Key source run id + step, so a resumed run produces the same key
Retry cap per tool a few attempts, with backoff
Retry budget per run one bad tool can't consume the whole run

stages.name: Prevent
stages.html:
"Fail fast on a dead dependency, and say so."

Breaker:closedopen: calls fail at oncehalf-open: one trialclosed

In my interviewer each dependency has a breaker: 5 failures open it, and the cooldown starts at 20 s and doubles up to 300 s. While it's open, calls fail immediately and the fallback path runs.

Output rule Example
Name unresolved failures "I found 3 of 5 invoices; billing timed out on the rest"
Label partial results as partial never present them as complete

Fix layer: tool contract for idempotency, runtime for retries and breakers.

followUps.question: Should the model or the runtime retry?
followUps.html:
The runtime for transient errors; the model only when the arguments must change.

Retry by Cost Use for
Runtime no tokens timeouts, rate limits
Model a full model call invalid arguments

followUps.question: "Just retry three times."
followUps.html:
Three retries of a non-idempotent payment is three payments.

  • Without idempotency, a retry is a bug.
  • With it, a retry is resilience.

followUps.question: 🧪 The tool timed out but the charge went through. The run resumes. What happens?
followUps.html:
It depends entirely on the key.

key from run + step:   retry → seen → "ch_0001" returned, 1 charge
random key per call:   retry → new key → second charge

followUps.question: How do you stop one flaky tool from sinking every run?
followUps.html:
Isolate it and define what "degraded" means per journey.

  • A breaker per tool.
  • A per-tool retry cap.
  • A degraded path: skip, use a fallback, or escalate to a person.

dontSay: "We retry until it works." — unbounded, and unsafe for side effects.
"No results" when the real story is "the tool failed". — say what failed.
"The model will handle the error." — only the class it can fix.

agentic-ai-q9.testing: hard stops in code, loop detection, and graceful partial output, plus the planning failures behind runaway loops.
agentic-ai-q9.trap: relying on the prompt to tell it to stop when it's done.
agentic-ai-q9.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Symptom "Step counts sit at the cap, the same call repeats, and cost per task spikes."
2 · Hypotheses "There are four usual reasons. The observation doesn't tell it to change strategy. The plan assumed a capability that doesn't exist. The steps succeed but don't converge on the goal. Or context truncation dropped the plan."
3 · Evidence "I read the trajectory, not the output, and find the first point where it repeated or left the plan. That point tells me which of the four it is."
4 · Root cause "Underneath all of them, nothing binding told it to stop. A prompt instruction is advisory; only limits in code and a finish action are binding."
5 · Fix "So the fix has layers. Hard bounds: a step cap, a token or spend budget, a wall-clock deadline. Detection: the same tool with the same arguments three times is a loop, and so is a state that stops changing. An explicit finish tool, or a goal check my code can run. And when anything trips, the run returns partial results and the reason."
6 · Prevent "Then budgets become product policy per journey, with alerts on cap hits, and I fix the cause the trace showed. The caps are the safety net, not the fix."
Close "Fixed means runs end by finishing, and the rare one that doesn't ends with something useful."

stages.name: Symptom
stages.html:
"Three signals, all visible in metrics before anyone reads a trace."

Signal Metric
Runs ending at the step cap cap-hit rate
The same call repeated repeated-signature count per run
Cost per task spiking tokens per run, p95

stages.name: Hypotheses
stages.html:
"Each reason leaves a different signature."

Reason Trace signature
Unhelpful observation same call, same error, repeated
Plan assumes a missing capability early steps fail, then improvisation
Goal drift steps succeed and don't converge
Context truncation the plan disappears; later steps are orphaned

stages.name: Evidence
stages.html:
"The first repeated or off-plan step classifies the failure."

Observation Likely cause Next action
Step 4 onward: identical call, identical error the error isn't actionable rewrite the tool's error message
Step 2 calls a tool that isn't there the plan assumed it add the tool, or tell the planner what exists
Every step "works", the answer never arrives no checkable goal a goal predicate or a finish contract
The plan is absent from context at step 12 truncation pin the plan; compact the rest

stages.name: Root cause
stages.claim: no stop signal the model can't ignore
stages.html:
"Advisory in the prompt, binding in code."

Requirement In the prompt Enforced outside
Stop when done "stop when you're done" a finish tool; a goal predicate
Don't loop "don't repeat yourself" repeated-signature detection
Stay within budget "be efficient" step, token, cost and time caps
Make progress — N steps with no new information → escalate or abort

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
"Loop detection is a counter over call signatures." Run with Python 3.12.

import json
from collections import Counter
def looping(history, repeats=3):
    sig = Counter(json.dumps(call, sort_keys=True) for call, _ in history)
    return any(n >= repeats for n in sig.values())
h = [(("search", {"q": "x"}), "none")] * 3
print(looping(h), looping(h[:2]))     # → True False
On detection:inject once "this call failed 3 times; try a different approach or finish"abortreturn partial results + reason

stages.name: Prevent
stages.html:
"Hitting a limit is a designed outcome, with its own user experience."

Control Practice
Step and cost budgets set per journey, from the eval distribution
Alerts cap-hit rate and loop detections per release
The cause fixed where the trace pointed: tool errors, planning, context

My interviewer's run budget ends the call with a fixed closing line and still produces feedback.

Fix layer: runtime budget for the stops; tool contract or context for the cause.

followUps.question: What should the user see when the cap trips?
followUps.html:
What was done, what wasn't, and why.

  • Example: "I found 3 of 5 invoices; the billing system timed out on the rest."
  • Never: an empty answer, or a confident one that hides the gap.

followUps.question: "Just raise the step limit."
followUps.html:
If it loops at 20 it loops at 50, at a higher cost.

Wrong order:cap hitraise the capsame loop, bigger bill
Right order:cap hitread the tracefix the causekeep the cap

followUps.question: 🧪 The agent alternates between two different calls forever. Does exact-repeat detection catch it?
followUps.html:
Only if it counts signatures across the whole history.

Detector A, B, A, B, A, B
Consecutive repeats only misses it
Counts per signature (as in the snippet) A appears 3 times: caught
No-progress rule catches what both miss

followUps.question: How do you set the cap?
followUps.html:
From the eval distribution, per journey.

cap = p99 steps of successful runs + headroom

Runs beyond that are almost always failures anyway.

dontSay: "The prompt tells it to stop when done." — advisory, not binding.
An abort that returns nothing. — partial results and a reason.
"We raised the limit and it went away." — the cause is still there.

agentic-ai-q10.testing: whether you know self-critique needs an external signal to add information.
agentic-ai-q10.trap: adding a reflection loop everywhere and calling it a quality improvement.
agentic-ai-q10.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision rule "It helps when there's something real to push against. Reflection loops work when there's an external signal: failing tests, a compiler error, a schema validator. The model turns that feedback into a correction and tries again."
2 · Reflection's real cost "Without that signal, it's the model grading its own work with the same weights that made the mistake. Research has shown models struggle to correct their own reasoning without external feedback, and can talk themselves out of right answers. And every round is another full call."
3 · No reflection's real cost "Skipping it has a cost too. Where a cheap verifier exists, not taking one retry against it leaves easy wins on the table."
4 · The tell "The tell is what changes between attempts. If the revisions mostly rephrase, and don't fix an error something flagged, the loop is rhetorical."
5 · What I'd pick "So I invest in verifiability first: tests, validators, checkable claims. Then one bounded retry against the verifier. In my interview system, scoring isn't reviewed by the model that produced it. Two independent assessors score the transcript and a reconciler settles differences from verbatim evidence."
Close "Reflection is only as good as its error signal."

stages.name: The decision rule
stages.html:
"The value of reflection follows the quality of the signal."

Signal Reflection value
Tests, a compiler, a validator high: real error information
A rubric checked by another model medium: depends on how the judge was calibrated
The same model re-reading its answer low, sometimes negative (Huang et al., 2023)
With a signal:attemptverifier reports a specific errorreviseverifier passes
Without:attempt"review your answer"a reworded attempt

Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) is the with-signal case: verbal feedback from the environment across trials.

stages.name: Reflection's real cost
stages.html:
"Before keeping a reflection loop, I fill in this table."

Metric No reflection 1 round 2 rounds
Task success on the eval set measure measure measure
Cost per task 1× about 2× about 3×
p95 latency measure measure measure
Answers changed from right to wrong — measure measure

The last row is the one people skip. A loop with no verifier can make a correct answer worse.

stages.name: No reflection's real cost
stages.html:
"Where a check is cheap and objective, one retry against it is worth having."

Task Cheap verifier One retry worth it?
Code change the test suite yes
Structured extraction the schema and business rules yes
A free-text essay none no; use a person or a calibrated judge

stages.name: The tell
stages.html:
"I diff attempt one against attempt two."

The revision… Verdict
Fixes the specific error the verifier reported the loop is working
Rephrases, adds caveats, changes tone rhetorical; remove the loop
Flips a correct answer harmful; remove the loop

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html:
"Build the check, then let the model use it once or twice."

Order:make the outcome checkableone retry against the checkmeasurestop at one or two rounds

For scoring in my interviewer, independence replaces self-review:

Role Sees Purpose
Assessor A the transcript, strict reading an independent score
Assessor B the transcript, evidence-first a second independent score
Reconciler both scores and verbatim evidence settles differences
Reviewer never reads the Panel's output a separate check

Fix layer: orchestration for the retry; the sensor is what makes it work.

followUps.question: Why does coding benefit most?
followUps.html:
The environment ships the verifier.

  • Tests and compilers give objective, cheap feedback after every attempt.
  • Version control makes every attempt reversible.

followUps.question: "Self-reflection always improves accuracy."
followUps.html:
Without external feedback, gains are small or negative, and cost rises each round.

With a verifier Without
Information added per round a specific error none
Cost per round one call one call

followUps.question: 🧪 Use a second model as the critic. Better?
followUps.html:
Somewhat, under two conditions.

  • Calibrated against human labels.
  • Different context from the worker.

Otherwise it shares the same blind spots and adds a judge's own biases.

followUps.question: How do reasoning models change this?
followUps.html:
They do some self-checking internally, so explicit loops matter mainly when the feedback is environmental.

Loop On a reasoning-class model
"Review your answer" mostly redundant
Retry against a failing test still valuable

dontSay: "Add a reflection step to improve quality" with no verifier. — there's nothing new to reflect on.
Unbounded refine loops. — most of the gain is in the first retry.
"The agent double-checks itself." — name the check.

agentic-ai-q11.testing: whether you separate what lives in the window from what survives sessions, and design the write policy, not just the stores.
agentic-ai-q11.trap: naming memory types with no write or retrieval policy: "append everything to the transcript".
agentic-ai-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask about the horizon: one task, or a relationship over months? How many users and tenants? And what's personal data that someone can ask me to delete?"
2 · Constraints and numbers "The window is a budget. The system prompt, tool schemas, retrieved memory, history and the scratchpad all compete for it, so memory gets a fixed share."
3 · Baseline design "There are three layers. Working memory is the context window, rebuilt each step. Run state is the checkpointed trajectory of this task, so a crash or an approval pause can resume. Long-term memory is external stores that survive sessions: episodic, meaning what happened before; semantic, meaning facts about the user or domain; and procedural, meaning playbooks that worked."
4 · Deep-dive "The write policy is the real design. I decide what's memorable, extract it into a schema, reconcile it with what's stored, and give it an expiry. On the read side, the top few relevant memories go into the prompt with their provenance, so the model can weigh how stale they are."
5 · Failure modes "It fails through noise from writing everything, contradictory facts, leaks across tenants, and poisoned memories written from untrusted content."
6 · Evolve "Then I track how often a retrieved memory is used and how often users correct it, and prune what's never used."
Close "Memory is a write policy with stores behind it, scoped per tenant and per user."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Three questions decide how much memory to build at all."

Question Changes
One task, or months of relationship? whether long-term stores are needed
How many users and tenants? the isolation model
What's personal data? deletion, retention, what may never be written

Earning it: a single-session task needs working memory and run state only.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Memory competes with everything else in the prompt."

window budget per step (illustrative)
system prompt + tool schemas   4,000 tokens   ← stable, cached
retrieved memory               1,000 tokens   ← a fixed share: top 3–5 items
recent history                 3,000 tokens
current observation + scratch  2,000 tokens

Latency: one memory read adds a lookup or a vector search before the model call, so it's on the critical path and needs its own time budget.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"Each layer has its own store, its own write rule and its own read rule."

Layer Holds Store Write Read
Working this step's context the prompt rebuilt each step —
Run state trajectory, plan progress a checkpointer (database) every step on resume
Episodic past cases and outcomes vector store on resolution similarity, top-k
Semantic facts about the user or domain key-value or SQL extracted and reconciled by key
Procedural playbooks that worked curated documents after review by task type

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"Writing is a pipeline with a gate at the front."

Write path:candidate factmemorable?extract into a schemareconcile with what's storedset expiry + provenancestore
Step Rule
Memorable facts the user stated, outcomes, corrections
Never written as fact raw tool output, model speculation, text from untrusted content
Reconcile "moved to Pune" replaces "lives in Delhi"; newest wins, with provenance kept
Read top few items, each tagged "from a conversation in March"

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Four ways memory makes the agent worse."

Failure Cause Control
Retrieval returns junk write-everything the memorability filter
Contradictory facts no reconciliation upsert by key; newest wins, with provenance
Cross-tenant leak a shared index tenant and user keys on every read
Poisoned memory injected content stored as fact write only from trusted sources; review
Requirement In the prompt Enforced outside
Only this user's memories never the query is filtered by tenant and user id
"Forget this" — deletion reaches every store

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"A memory that's never used is cost and risk with no benefit."

Metric Action
Share of retrieved memories used in the answer prune what's never used
User corrections of remembered facts fix reconciliation or expiry
Recall across sessions, on scripted cases the release gate

Evaluation hook: scripted multi-session cases. Fix layer: memory in the harness.

followUps.question: Why not just keep the whole transcript?
followUps.html:
Cost grows every turn and quality falls as stale, contradictory history piles up.

Instead:recent turns verbatimolder turns summariseddurable facts externalised

followUps.question: "A vector store is our memory."
followUps.html:
A vector store is one backend, and the wrong one for current facts.

Need Store
"What's this user's plan tier now?" keyed store: update and delete by key
"Have we seen a case like this?" vector store: similarity

Similarity search can't reliably return "the current value".

followUps.question: 🧪 A user says "forget my address". What must happen?
followUps.html:
Deletion has to reach every place the fact lives.

  • Semantic store: delete the key.
  • Episodic records and caches: remove or scrub.
  • Extraction: stop it being re-learned from old transcripts.
  • Traces: covered by their own retention rule.

followUps.question: How would you evaluate memory?
followUps.html:
With scripted multi-session cases.

Case Checks
A fact from session 1 is needed in session 3 recall
A correction in session 2 the old value is gone
Another user's fact is relevant it is not returned

dontSay: "We append every message to memory." — that's a transcript, and it drowns retrieval.
Memory with no tenant scoping. — isolation is a privacy boundary.
"It remembers everything." — say what it writes, and what it never writes.

agentic-ai-q12.testing: whether you budget the window deliberately and know why long runs degrade.
agentic-ai-q12.trap: appending every observation and blaming the model when step 30 is worse than step 5.
agentic-ai-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Context engineering is deciding what occupies the window at each step: system prompt, tool schemas, retrieved facts, history, scratchpad. In an agent the prompt is rebuilt every turn, and most of it isn't written by me."
2 · How it works "Whatever is in the window is the model's whole world for that step. The occupants compete for space, and position matters: models use the middle of a long context less reliably than the ends."
3 · Prove it "The arithmetic shows the cost of doing nothing. With a three-thousand-token base and eight hundred tokens added per step, ten steps of append-everything is about sixty-nine thousand tokens. Compacting after step five saves about two and a half thousand tokens on every later step."
4 · What it costs or breaks "Context rot is what happens without it. Stale observations, dead ends and superseded facts pile up, contradictions appear, and the instruction from step one gets buried. Decisions get worse and each step costs more."
5 · So what for the system "So I budget the window like memory: compact older turns, keep a running summary of facts and failed attempts, truncate tool outputs, re-retrieve instead of retaining, and give sub-tasks their own context."
Close "In my interviewer the speaker sees only the last eight messages; the plan lives in state, not in the prompt."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Prompt engineering writes a string; context engineering writes the policy that assembles one, every step."

Occupant Written by
System prompt, tool schemas me
Retrieved documents and memories a retriever
History the model and the user
Tool observations external systems

Everything not in the window has to be retrieved or held in state.

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
"Two forces: there's a fixed budget, and not every position is read equally."

Assembly, each step:stable prefixretrieved factscompacted historyrecent turnscurrent observation
Force Consequence
A finite window every occupant's share is a decision
Weaker use of the middle (Liu et al., 2023, Lost in the Middle) key instructions go at the ends, or are pinned
Every token is re-sent each step length costs money and latency on every step

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
"3,000-token base, each step adds 800, about 300 output."

append everything, 10 steps:  10 × 3,000 + 800 × 45 + 10 × 300 = 69,000 tokens
append everything,  5 steps:   5 × 3,000 + 800 × 10 +  5 × 300 = 24,500 tokens

compact to a 1,500-token summary after step 5:
  step i (i ≥ 6) re-sends 3,000 + 1,500 + 800 × (i − 6)
  instead of             3,000 + 800 × (i − 1)
  saving per late step = 800 × 5 − 1,500 = 2,500 tokens

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
"Rot has recognisable symptoms, and none of them raises an error."

Symptom Cause
Late steps contradict early facts superseded observations still in context
The agent repeats a dead end failed attempts never summarised as "tried, failed"
Instructions ignored late in a run buried mid-context
Rising cost and latency per step accumulated history re-sent

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
"Five levers, applied at thresholds, not every step."

Lever What it does
Compact at a token threshold older turns become a structured summary
A running "facts so far / tried and failed" block keeps decisions, drops the working
Truncate tool outputs keep the extracted result, not the payload
Re-retrieve, don't retain fetch again when needed
Isolate sub-tasks a sub-agent gets a clean window and returns a compact artefact

Compacting rewrites the prefix, which is a cache write, so it's done in batches.

My interviewer: RECENT_TURNS = 8 for the speaker; the plan, delivered moves and insights live in typed state and are injected only when needed.

Fix layer: context assembly in the harness.

followUps.question: Doesn't a million-token window fix this?
followUps.html:
It raises the ceiling, not the quality.

Bigger window Still true
More fits positional effects and contradictions remain
No truncation every token costs latency and money on every step

followUps.question: What do you lose by summarising?
followUps.html:
Whatever the summary dropped, so I keep the raw data elsewhere.

  • Store raw history in the run store, so it can be re-retrieved.
  • Summarise decisions and facts, not just text.

followUps.question: 🧪 Step 25 ignores a constraint stated at step 1. Fix?
followUps.html:
Pin it; don't rely on step-1 history surviving.

Fragile:constraint lives in turn 1compaction or distancelost
Robust:constraint in the system prompt or a fixed "task contract" blockre-inserted every step

followUps.question: How does multi-agent relate?
followUps.html:
Sub-agents are a context-isolation tool.

Honest reason to split Not a reason
A clean window per sub-task, compact artefact back different persona prompts over the same context

dontSay: "Context is free with large windows." — it's paid for on every step.
"We pass the full history every step." — that's how rot starts.
"The model forgot." — say what was in the window and where.

agentic-ai-q13.testing: durable execution: checkpoints, idempotent side effects, and state schema versioning.
agentic-ai-q13.trap: in-memory agent state, which works in the demo and loses money in production.
agentic-ai-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "It depends entirely on where the state lives. In memory, the run is gone: tokens spent, side effects half-applied, and the user starts again. Checkpointed outside the pod, a new worker resumes from the last completed step."
2 · Trace the mechanism "The dangerous moment is a crash between an action and its checkpoint. The refund went through at the provider, the pod died before saving, and on resume the same step runs again."
3 · The rule that decides it "So the rule is that a resume can replay the step that was in flight. Side-effecting tools have to be idempotent, with a key derived from the run and the step, so the replay returns the first result."
4 · Variants that flip it "The same mechanism covers other cases: an approval that takes two days, where the run is parked with no worker held, and a deploy mid-run, where the state schema needs a version so in-flight runs aren't orphaned."
5 · The production version "In production, runs are durable work items: a queue, stateless workers, and checkpoints in a store, so any worker can resume any run. In my interviewer, graph writes are keyed by turn and overwritten, so re-running a turn replaces it. A live voice call can't resume invisibly, though, so the design scores the partial transcript and offers a resume."
Close "State outside the pod, and idempotent side effects; then a restart costs one repeated step."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
"Two outcomes, decided before the crash."

State lives After the restart
In the agent object, in memory the run is lost; side effects may be half-applied
In an external checkpoint store resumes from the last saved step; the in-flight step may repeat

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.claim: a crash between action and checkpoint
stages.html:
"The gap is one step wide."

Step Event Checkpoint
4 issue_refund(o-42, 30) sent —
4 the refund succeeds at the provider —
4 pod killed before saving last saved = step 3
resume step 4 re-runs issue_refund(o-42, 30) —
result a double refund, unless the call carries key run-91:step-4 saved = step 4

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
"Side effects aren't transactional with run state, so the replay has to be harmless."

Without a key:resumestep 4 againsecond refund
With a key:resumestep 4 again with run-91:step-4provider returns the first receipt
Property of the key Why
Derived from run id + step a resumed run computes the same key
Not random per call a random key makes every replay look new

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
"Durable execution gives three things at once: crash recovery, long pauses and replay for debugging."

Variant What must hold
Approval pending for 2 days the run is parked in the store; no worker held
A deploy changes the state schema a version field + migration, or old runs pinned to old workers
An external call takes 10 minutes an asynchronous continuation, not a held connection
Two workers pick up the same run a lease with expiry; idempotent tools as the backstop

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
"Workers are stateless; the run is a row in a store."

Path:requestqueueany workerstepcheckpointnext step, on any worker
Detail
Built LangGraph checkpoints keyed by turn and overwritten, so pre-emptive re-runs are idempotent; post-call scoring has its own budget
Designed scoring behind a durable queue, so a dead pod can't lose the scorecard
Honest limit a live voice interview can't resume transparently: turns are flushed, the partial transcript is scored, a resume is offered

Fix layer: orchestration for checkpoints, tool contract for idempotency.

followUps.question: What exactly goes in the checkpoint?
followUps.html:
Enough to resume and to replay for debugging.

  • Messages, tool calls and results.
  • Plan progress and typed state fields.
  • The bundle version (prompt, tools, model) that produced them.

followUps.question: "Retries handle crashes."
followUps.html:
Retrying the run repeats everything; resuming repeats one step.

Retry the whole run Resume from a checkpoint
Side effects all repeated at most one, and idempotent
Tokens paid again only the remaining steps

followUps.question: 🧪 Two workers resume the same run. What stops a double execution?
followUps.html:
A lease first, idempotency second.

worker A takes a lease on run-91 (expires in 60 s)   ← B sees the lease and backs off
if the lease logic fails: both call issue_refund with key run-91:step-4
                                                      ← the provider applies it once

followUps.question: How does this change capacity planning?
followUps.html:
Workers scale horizontally; the state store is the thing to size.

Component Planning
Workers stateless; drain them on deploy
State store write rate = runs × steps; size and latency matter

dontSay: "State is in the agent object." — then a restart loses the run.
Resume without idempotency. — the in-flight step will repeat.
"We'll just retry the request." — that repeats every side effect.
