agentic-ai-q51.testing: that you stack graders by cost and trust, and that a judge is a model with a prompt that has to be validated against people.
agentic-ai-q51.trap: "An LLM judge scores each run from 1 to 5", with no calibration.
agentic-ai-q51.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision rule "I use the cheapest grader that can actually check the property. Code for anything about state, tool calls and constraints. A model-based judge for what needs reading. People to calibrate the judge and to settle what the other two can't."
2 · What code graders cost "Code graders are fast, free and reproducible. Their cost is brittleness: they fail valid variations, so I write them against outcomes and constraints, not exact wording or an exact path."
3 · What judges cost "A judge handles nuance, and it's non-deterministic, costs a model call, and has biases: position, verbosity, a preference for its own style. And it can be wrong consistently, which looks like reliability."
4 · The tell "I know a judge is good when it agrees with human labels on a held-out set at a rate I've measured, and when I've read its disagreements. Until then its score is an opinion."
5 · What I'd pick "So each trial goes through a stack. Outcome check, then trajectory assertions, and only if those pass does the judge look at the parts left over, with a narrow rubric. People label a sample every cycle to keep the judge honest."
Close "Code decides what it can; the judge is used narrowly and checked against people."

stages.name: The decision rule
stages.claim: the cheapest grader that can check it
stages.html:
"Three grader types, each with a job."

Code-based Model-based Human
Examples final-state check, tests, tool-call assertions rubric, pairwise, natural-language assertions expert review, spot checks
Strength fast, cheap, objective, reproducible flexible, handles open-ended output the gold standard
Weakness brittle to valid variation non-deterministic, needs calibration slow, expensive
Use for outcome and constraints tone, helpfulness, faithfulness to sources calibrating the judge; hard cases

The types and trade-offs follow Anthropic's eval guidance (Jan 2026).

stages.name: What code graders cost
stages.html:
"A code grader is only as good as the property it checks."

Brittle check Robust check
The reply equals a gold string the record exists with the right fields
Tools were called in this exact order required tools used; forbidden ones not
Exactly four steps within the step and cost budget
The reply contains "refunded" the refund is in the database

The last row matters most: an agent can say it did something that never happened, so I check the state.

stages.name: What judges cost
stages.claim: a model with its own errors
stages.html:
"A judge is a prompt, so it gets the same engineering as any prompt."

Bias Control
Position (favours first or second) run both orders; count only consistent verdicts
Verbosity (longer looks better) the rubric says length isn't quality; cap length in code
Self-preference a different model family as judge where possible
Scale compression (everything is a 4) pairwise, or a binary rubric per criterion
Whole-trajectory overload judge one narrow question, on the relevant slice of the transcript

Agreement between strong judges and people has been measured at about 80% on pairwise preference, close to the rate between people (Zheng et al., 2023, MT-Bench). That's a reference point, not a guarantee for my rubric.

stages.name: The tell
stages.html:
"Calibration is a small, repeatable procedure."

Calibrate:people label 100–200 trialsjudge labels the same, blindagreement rateread the disagreementsfix the rubricre-measure on a held-out set
Calibration result Decision
Agreement about as high as person-to-person usable as a gate
Lower, with a pattern fix the rubric; split the criterion
Lower, no pattern the property isn't judge-able yet; keep people on it

In my interview-agent design this is "score the scorer": the evaluator runs against a hand-labelled reference set and is gated on inter-assessor agreement ≥ 0.8 and score reproducibility ≥ 95% on re-run. Measured so far on provisional labels (26 Sep 2026): repeatability std 0.05 and 12 of 12 bias traps passed, but MAE 1.02 and 54% within ±1. So it's consistent and not yet calibrated, which is exactly the gap this stage is about.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: a stack, with the judge last
stages.html:
"Code filters first, so the judge only sees trials worth judging."

trial = {"tools": ["lookup_order", "refund"], "refund_amount": 40,
         "db": {"order_17": "refunded"}, "reply": "Done, I've refunded order 17."}
def outcome(t): return t["db"].get("order_17") == "refunded"               # code: the final state
def trajectory(t): return "delete_account" not in t["tools"] and t["refund_amount"] <= 50 and len(t["tools"]) <= 6
def grade(t):
    checks = {"outcome": outcome(t), "trajectory": trajectory(t)}
    return checks, "send reply to judge: tone, clarity" if all(checks.values()) else "fail, no judge call"
print(grade(trial))
# → ({'outcome': True, 'trajectory': True}, 'send reply to judge: tone, clarity')
trial["db"] = {}                                                           # the reply says refunded; nothing changed
print(grade(trial))
# → ({'outcome': False, 'trajectory': True}, 'fail, no judge call')

In the second trial the reply still reads well. A judge reading only the reply would pass it; the state check fails it for free.

Scoring Use
Binary: all graders must pass regression suites and safety constraints
Weighted, with a threshold capability suites with partial credit

Fix layer: eval. The judge's prompt and model are versioned; changing either changes the metric.

followUps.question: "The judge gave the new version 4.4, up from 4.1."
followUps.html:
That's not evidence yet.

Missing Why it matters
Agreement with human labels the scale may not track quality
Run-to-run spread of the judge 0.3 may be inside its noise
A pairwise comparison steadier than two absolute scores

followUps.question: 🧪 The judge agrees with people on 90 of 100 trials, and 85 of those 100 are passes. Is 90% good?
followUps.html:
Less than it looks: always saying "pass" would score 85%.

judge agreement:          90 / 100
"always pass" baseline:   85 / 100       ← only 5 points better than no judge
look at the 15 true failures: how many did the judge catch?

I report agreement on the failure class separately; that's the number that protects a release.

followUps.question: How would you improve a weak judge?
followUps.html:
Narrow the question before changing the model.

  • Split the rubric: one criterion per call, binary.
  • Show less: the relevant slice of the transcript, not all of it.
  • Add labelled examples of borderline passes and fails.
  • Then try a stronger judge model, and re-calibrate.

followUps.question: When must a person stay in the loop?
followUps.html:
Where there's no fast, objective check and the stakes are high.

Property Grader
Taste, research quality, long-horizon judgement people, sampled
Irreversible or regulated decisions people, every time

followUps.question: Judging every trial doubles the eval bill. How do you control it?
followUps.html:
Let code remove trials before the judge sees them, and sample the rest.

Cost path:all trialscode graders (free)judge on survivorspeople on a sample of judge verdicts

dontSay: "We use LLM-as-judge." — say what it agrees with, and how often.
"The judge reads the whole trajectory and scores it." — one narrow question at a time.
"The agent confirmed it completed the task." — check the state.
"Human review doesn't scale, so we dropped it." — it's what calibrates everything else.

links.label: Component vs end to end eval

agentic-ai-q52.testing: a repeatable method: contain, pull the trace, diff against a good run, find the first divergent step, classify model or harness, and leave a regression case.
agentic-ai-q52.trap: "I'd look at the logs and tweak the prompt."
agentic-ai-q52.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Symptom "First I contain it: pause the agent or the tool involved, and note what it did to real systems. Then I state the symptom precisely: which run, which action, what should have happened."
2 · Hypotheses "For a production agent my hypotheses are few: something changed, such as a prompt, a model snapshot or a tool; an input we'd never seen; a tool returned something odd; or the context was polluted earlier in the run."
3 · Evidence "I pull the trace for that run: every model call and tool call as spans, with inputs, outputs, tokens and the versions that ran. Then I find a successful run of the same task type and compare them step by step."
4 · Root cause "The useful point is the first step where the bad run diverges from the good one. Everything after that is a consequence. At that step I ask whether the model had what it needed. If it did, it's a model failure. If not, it's the harness."
5 · Fix "The fix goes in the layer that failed: a tool contract, a validator, a missing piece of context, a budget. I reproduce it with a replay of the recorded run before and after the change."
6 · Prevent "And the failing run becomes a regression case, with an alert on the pattern."
Close "Fixed means the replay passes, the case is in the suite, and there's an alert for the pattern."

stages.name: Symptom
stages.html:
"Before diagnosing, stop it doing more of the same."

First ten minutes:pause the agent or the toollist side effects on real systemsidentify the run idwrite the symptom in one sentence
Vague Precise
"The agent went crazy" "Run r-8841 issued three refunds of 400 on order 17; policy limit is 50"
"It's slow tonight" "p95 steps per run went from 6 to 19 after 02:10"

stages.name: Hypotheses
stages.html:
"Four families, each checkable from the trace."

Hypothesis Check in the trace
A release: prompt, tool definition, model snapshot versions stamped on the run against the last good run
A new kind of input the first user or tool input; is it in the eval set?
A tool misbehaved: error, timeout, changed schema tool spans: status, latency, payload shape
Polluted context: an earlier error or injected text what was in the context at the failing step

stages.name: Evidence
stages.claim: the span tree, and a good run to compare
stages.html:
"A trace is a tree of spans; I read it top down."

invoke_agent  run r-8841  prompt v17 · model snapshot m-0915     19 steps · 61,200 tokens
├─ model call   plan                              420 ms   1,900 tok
├─ execute_tool lookup_order(id=17)               110 ms   ok
├─ model call   decide                            380 ms   2,400 tok
├─ execute_tool refund(amount=400)                 95 ms   ok        ← no check_policy before it
├─ model call   decide                            390 ms   3,100 tok
├─ execute_tool refund(amount=400)                 97 ms   ok        ← same call again
└─ … 13 more steps, same pattern

The trace is illustrative. What each span must carry: inputs and outputs, tokens, latency, status, and the prompt, tool and model versions. Span names follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (invoke_agent, execute_tool), which are still marked as in development as of Oct 2026.

stages.name: Root cause
stages.html:
"I diff the bad run against a good one and stop at the first difference."

from collections import Counter
good = [("plan", "lookup_order"), ("lookup_order", "id=17"), ("check_policy", "limit=50"), ("refund", "40")]
bad  = [("plan", "lookup_order"), ("lookup_order", "id=17"), ("refund", "400"), ("refund", "400"), ("refund", "400")]
def first_divergence(a, b):
    for i, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(a, b)):
        if x != y: return i, x, y
i, x, y = first_divergence(good, bad)
print(f"step {i}: good={x} bad={y}")                          # → step 2: good=('check_policy', 'limit=50') bad=('refund', '400')
print([step for step, n in Counter(bad).items() if n >= 3])   # → [('refund', '400')]
At the divergent step Verdict
The policy tool was missing from the tool list after a release harness: a tool-definition change
The policy text wasn't in context harness: context assembly
Everything was present and the model skipped the check model; and the check shouldn't be optional
A tool result contained instructions injection; treat observations as data

Whichever it is, two harness gaps are already visible: the refund tool accepted 400 against a limit of 50, and the same call ran three times.

stages.name: Fix
stages.claim: in the layer that failed, proven by replay
stages.html:
"I fix the enforcement before the wording."

Requirement In the prompt Enforced outside
Refunds within the limit the policy, for explanation the refund tool rejects amounts over the limit
No repeated side effects — an idempotency key per order and action
No runaway loops — a repeated (tool, args) detector and a step budget
Policy check before refund guidance the refund tool requires a policy-check token
Verify:replay the recorded run with model and tool outputs frozenapply the fixreplayrun the full regression suite

A replay only reproduces the run if the model and tool boundaries are frozen; re-executing live gives a new trajectory.

stages.name: Prevent
stages.claim: a regression case and an alert
stages.html:
"Every incident leaves two things behind."

Artefact Content
Regression task this input, graded on the final state: one refund, within the limit
Alert repeated identical tool calls; steps or cost per run over budget; tool-argument rejections
Release note which version introduced it; the canary that would have caught it

In my interview-agent design, prompt_version and model_version are pinned per session precisely so a bad session maps to an exact configuration. Built in the prototype: per-run budgets for calls and tokens, and a circuit breaker per dependency (5 failures open it, cooldown from 20 s doubling to 300 s).

Fix layer: tool contract and runtime budget first, prompt/context second.

followUps.question: "Just read the application logs."
followUps.html:
Flat logs lose the structure that explains an agent failure.

Logs Traces
Lines in time order, across requests one tree per run
No parent and child which model call led to which tool call
Rarely the full prompt inputs, outputs, tokens, versions per span

followUps.question: 🧪 In the snippet, the runs first differ at step 2. Why not look at step 4, where the loop becomes obvious?
followUps.html:
Because step 4 is a consequence.

step 2: check_policy skipped        ← cause: the first divergence
step 2–4: refund(400) × 3           ← consequences: no limit, no idempotency, no loop detector

Fixing only the loop would leave one wrong refund of 400.

followUps.question: There's no good run to compare with. Now what?
followUps.html:
Compare against the specification of the task.

  • Expected postconditions from the eval task for that journey.
  • A fresh run on the same input in a sandbox, several times.
  • The previous release, replayed on the same input.

followUps.question: You can't reproduce it. Was it a one-off?
followUps.html:
Unknown until I measure the rate.

Step Purpose
Run the same input N times in a sandbox get a failure rate, not an anecdote
Search traces for the same pattern see how often it already happened
Keep the stored trace as evidence a re-run needn't match it

followUps.question: How do you make 3 a.m. debugging possible in the first place?
followUps.html:
Decide the trace schema before launch.

  • Every span: inputs, outputs, tokens, latency, status, versions.
  • Every run: a run id that links to the user request and the side effects.
  • Retention and redaction set up front, so the trace exists and is safe to open.

dontSay: "I'd tweak the prompt and redeploy." — no cause, no test, and the tool still accepts 400.
"The model hallucinated." — say what it was given at the divergent step.
"It works when I try it." — one run isn't a rate.
"We'll watch it closely." — add the regression case and the alert.

agentic-ai-q53.testing: that you alert on agent behaviour and quality, not only uptime, and that you treat trace storage as a sized, tiered, privacy-controlled system.
agentic-ai-q53.trap: "We log everything and have a dashboard for latency and errors."
agentic-ai-q53.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what the agent can change in the world, what a bad hour looks like for the business, and what the data in the prompts contains, because that sets both the alerts and the privacy rules."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Then I'd size it. An agent run is dozens of spans, and the payloads are whole prompts. At a million runs a day, keeping everything is terabytes a month. So full capture for all runs isn't the plan."
3 · Baseline design "The design has two tiers. Metadata for every span: names, timings, tokens, status, versions. Full payloads for all errors and a sample of normal runs. Alerts sit on four groups: behaviour, quality, cost and latency, and safety."
4 · Deep-dive "The agent-specific alerts are the ones a normal service doesn't have: repeated identical tool calls, steps per run, budget exhaustion, tool-argument rejections, escalation rate, and a sampled quality score from an online judge."
5 · Failure modes "What goes wrong: alert noise from run-to-run variance, a sampling rule that drops the rare failure, personal data sitting in traces, and a judge that drifts unnoticed."
6 · Evolve "Over time the traces feed the eval set: flagged runs become test cases. And I'd instrument against the open telemetry conventions so the backend can change."
Close "Every run is measured, the interesting runs are kept in full, and each alert is a behaviour someone can act on."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"The alerts follow from what a bad hour costs."

Question Sets
What can the agent write, send or spend? which behaviours page a person
Who is the user, and what's in their messages? redaction and retention
Interactive or background? latency thresholds
How many runs a day, how many steps each? storage and sampling
Any regulatory retention rules? what must be kept, and for how long

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"I size the store before choosing what to keep."

40 spans per run × 5 KB payload per span = 200 KB per run             (illustrative)
1,000,000 runs a day → 200 GB a day → 6 TB for 30 days                ← keep everything

tiered:
metadata for all spans: 40 × 0.3 KB = 12 KB per run → 12 GB a day
full payloads for errors + a sample (8% of runs): 0.08 × 200 GB = 16 GB a day
total 28 GB a day → 840 GB for 30 days                                 ← about 14% of full capture

Budget per request: tracing adds no model tokens. Spans are exported asynchronously, so the latency target for instrumentation is single-digit milliseconds per run (illustrative), and an exporter outage must never fail a user request.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: two tiers and four alert groups
stages.html:
"Measure everything, keep the interesting runs in full."

Alert group Signals
Behaviour steps per run, repeated identical tool calls, budget exhaustion, tool error and rejection rates
Quality sampled online-judge score, guardrail trips, escalation and retry rates
Cost and latency cost per successful task, tokens per run, p95 run time, cache-read share
Safety blocked actions, approvals pending or bypassed, injection flags

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: the alerts a normal service doesn't have
stages.html:
"An agent can be 'up', fast and returning 200s while doing the wrong thing."

Signal Why it's agent-specific Page or ticket
Same (tool, args) three times in a run a loop; cost and side effects multiply page
Runs ending on a budget limit the task isn't converging ticket; page on a spike
Tool-argument rejections the model is calling tools wrongly: a description or release problem ticket
Steps per run, p95 drift in how hard tasks have become ticket
Sampled judge score, per route and version quality with no error to catch ticket; page on a sharp drop
Escalation or user-retry rate users saying it didn't work ticket
Blocked irreversible action a control fired; someone should know page

Every signal is cut by prompt version, tool version and model snapshot. Without that, an alert says "something got worse" and not what changed.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Four ways the observability itself fails."

Failure Cause Control
Alert fatigue thresholds inside normal run-to-run variance thresholds from a measured baseline; alert on rates over windows
The rare failure wasn't kept uniform random sampling always keep errors, flagged runs, budget hits and new-version canaries
Personal data in traces prompts and tool results stored raw redact before storage; role-based access; short retention for payloads
The online judge drifted judge model or prompt changed version the judge; re-check agreement with human labels on a schedule
Storage bill surprise payloads kept for all spans tiering as above; some backends bill by span type
Tracing took the agent down synchronous export asynchronous export with a drop policy

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"Monitoring finds failure types the offline set didn't contain; those become tasks."

Loop:live trafficalerts and sampled scoringtriage flagged runsnew eval tasksrelease gate
Decision Practice
Instrumentation OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (gen_ai.*, invoke_agent, execute_tool); still in development as of Oct 2026, so pin the version
Backend swappable if the instrumentation is standard
Human feedback corrections are the highest-value signal: they're labels
Review someone reads a sample of transcripts every week

My interview-agent design names its health metrics before launch: speculative_hit_rate (target ≥ 70%), event_loop_lag_ms (alert at 50 ms) and the mix of move sources, with alerts wired before real candidates see it. Per-turn logs exist in the prototype.

Evaluation hook: the weekly count of production runs promoted into the eval set. Fix layer: infra and eval.

followUps.question: "The service is healthy: no 5xx, p95 is fine."
followUps.html:
Service health and agent health are different things.

Service metric Says nothing about
HTTP status a wrong tool chosen three steps back
Request latency steps and cost per task
Uptime whether the task was done

followUps.question: 🧪 You sample 5% of runs at random and the bad behaviour occurs in 1 run in 2,000. How many do you keep per million runs?
followUps.html:
About 25 of 500, unless the keep rule knows about the pattern.

bad runs per 1,000,000 = 1,000,000 / 2,000 = 500
kept by a 5% random sample = 500 × 0.05 = 25
kept by "always keep flagged runs" = 500, if a metadata rule flags them

That's why metadata is kept for every span: the keep decision is made from it.

followUps.question: How do you replay a trace?
followUps.html:
Serve the recorded model and tool outputs back, so the run is deterministic.

Technique Use
Record and replay (boundaries frozen) regression: did a change break this?
Re-run live from a checkpoint debugging and what-if; not a regression test

followUps.question: A customer asks you to delete their data. What about the traces?
followUps.html:
They're in scope, so the store has to support it.

  • Index traces by user or tenant id.
  • Short payload retention shrinks the problem.
  • Eval cases built from traces are scrubbed or synthesised before they're kept long term.

followUps.question: Build the observability stack or buy it?
followUps.html:
Buy the store and the UI; own the instrumentation, the alerts and the eval loop.

Part Choice
Trace store, viewer a product, or open source you operate
Instrumentation standard open, so the backend can change
What to alert on, what to keep yours: it encodes the product's risks

dontSay: "We log every prompt and response." — say how much that is, who can read it and for how long.
"We monitor latency and errors." — add steps, loops, budget hits and quality.
"We sample 1% of traces." — and always keep the errors and flagged runs.
"The judge score is our quality metric." — calibrated against whom, and when last?

agentic-ai-q54.testing: that you know what a benchmark actually grades, what a single score hides, and that you'd choose with your own tasks.
agentic-ai-q54.trap: "Model X is at the top of the leaderboard, so we'll use it."
agentic-ai-q54.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "SWE-bench gives an agent a real GitHub issue and a repository, and grades the patch by running the repository's tests: the ones that failed before must pass. It's execution-based, which is its strength."
2 · The line that matters "The score is a property of a model, a harness and a task set together. It isn't a property of the model alone, and it isn't a measure of my codebase."
3 · What it costs "So it misleads in specific ways. The issues are public, so they may be in training data. The repositories are a small set of open-source Python projects. Passing the tests isn't the same as a correct, maintainable change. And one pass rate hides consistency and cost."
4 · How I've used it "I use a public benchmark as a shortlist. The decision comes from a small suite of my own tasks, in my repository, with my tools, run several times, with cost and steps recorded next to success."
5 · Adjacent concept "The related idea is consistency: a benchmark that reports the chance that all k runs succeed tells me far more about a production agent than one that reports a single pass."
Close "A leaderboard tells me who to test; my own tasks tell me who to ship."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"Each benchmark is an environment plus a way of checking."

Benchmark Task Verified by
SWE-bench patch a real GitHub issue (about 2,294 tasks, 12 Python repositories) the repository's fail-to-pass tests
SWE-bench Verified 500 of those, human-checked same
GAIA tool-use questions with short answers exact match on the answer
WebArena tasks on sandboxed websites the final state of the environment
τ-bench a tool-using agent talking to a simulated customer final database state, and pass^k across repeats

Figures from the vault's benchmark note. The exact counts matter less than the two columns: what's attempted and how it's checked.

stages.name: The line that matters
stages.claim: a score belongs to model + harness + tasks
stages.html:
"Three things produce the number, and only one of them is the model."

Score:modelharness (tools, context policy, retries, budget)task setgraderone percentage
Change only this The score moves because
The harness better tools or more attempts, same model
The budget more steps and tokens per task
The task subset easier or cleaner tasks

Evaluating an agent means evaluating the harness and the model together (Anthropic, Jan 2026). A leaderboard row that doesn't name the harness and the budget can't be compared with another.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html:
"Each gap is a question I'd ask before believing the number."

Gap What it hides What I ask
Contamination public issues and fixes may be in the training data how does it do on tasks created after the model's cut-off?
Narrow distribution open-source Python; not my language, monorepo or build system how does it do on my repository?
Tests as the oracle a patch can pass and still be wrong, unsafe or unmaintainable who reviewed the diffs?
One pass rate no consistency, no cost, no steps what's pass^k, and the cost per solved task?
Saturation scores bunch near the top and stop separating systems is there headroom left?
Harness-specific the result came from someone else's scaffold which harness and budget produced it?

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.html:
"The decision table has my tasks in its rows."

Candidate (model + harness) My tasks solved, pass^3 Cost per solved task Steps p95 Diffs accepted in review
A measure measure measure measure
B measure measure measure measure
My suite Detail
20–50 real tasks closed issues and bugs from my own repository, with their tests
Fresh written after the candidates' training cut-offs where possible
Graded on tests pass, nothing else breaks, and a person accepts the diff on a sample

The same logic in my own work: the interviewer's scoring is judged on my labelled goldens, not on a public leaderboard, and those goldens say "consistent, not yet calibrated" (std 0.05, MAE 1.02, provisional labels, 26 Sep 2026).

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"A single pass says it can; pass^k says it reliably does."

per-trial success 75%
pass@3 (any of 3)  = 1 − 0.25³ = 0.98
pass^3 (all of 3)  = 0.75³     = 0.42      ← what a user who repeats the task experiences

Once a benchmark becomes a target, systems get tuned to it, and the score drifts away from general ability. That's why I rotate my own held-out tasks and don't publish them.

Fix layer: model and harness selection, decided by eval on my distribution.

followUps.question: "It tops the leaderboard, so it's the best coding agent for us."
followUps.html:
It's the best on that task set, with that harness and budget.

Leaderboard says I still need
Highest pass rate results on my repository
One number consistency and cost
A model name the harness that produced it

followUps.question: 🧪 Agent A solves 60% at 1 unit of cost per task; agent B solves 66% at 3 units. Which is cheaper per solved task?
followUps.html:
A, by a wide margin.

A: 1 / 0.60 = 1.67 units per solved task
B: 3 / 0.66 = 4.55 units per solved task     ← 2.7× the cost for 6 more points

Whether six points are worth it depends on what an unsolved task costs me.

followUps.question: The tests pass. Why isn't that enough?
followUps.html:
Tests check the cases someone wrote, not the change as a whole.

  • Over-fitting to the test: special-casing the failing input.
  • Collateral damage: behaviour no test covers.
  • Maintainability: a passing patch nobody would merge.

followUps.question: How do you check for contamination?
followUps.html:
Use tasks the model can't have seen.

Check Signal
Tasks created after the training cut-off a drop against older tasks suggests memorisation
Private tasks from my own repository never public, so never trained on

followUps.question: A vendor shows a benchmark slide. What do you ask?
followUps.html:
Four questions, then a trial on my tasks.

  • Which harness, budget and number of attempts?
  • Which subset, and how many runs per task?
  • Cost and time per solved task?
  • Can we run it on thirty of our own issues this week?

dontSay: "The model scores X% on SWE-bench." — the model in which harness, with what budget?
"It passed the tests, so the fix is right." — tests are an oracle with gaps.
"Benchmarks are useless." — they're a fair shortlist.
"We picked the top one." — on whose tasks?

agentic-ai-q55.testing: that a passing suite is a claim about the suite, and that you'd check the suite against production before touching the agent.
agentic-ai-q55.trap: "The evals are green, so it must be a user-perception problem."
agentic-ai-q55.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Symptom "The suite is green and steady, while production signals are getting worse: more escalations, more retries, lower sampled quality scores. So one of the two measurements is wrong about the other."
2 · Hypotheses "Either production changed and the suite didn't, or the suite never measured what matters. That's traffic drift, a saturated suite, a judge that passes things users reject, a model or tool that changed underneath us, or an environment gap between the test rig and the real systems."
3 · Evidence "I'd compare the two distributions: cluster recent production runs by intent and check how many of those clusters the suite covers. And I'd take failing production traces and run them through the offline graders."
4 · Root cause "If the graders pass runs that users rejected, the graders are wrong. If the failing runs are a kind of task the suite doesn't contain, the suite is stale. The versions on the traces tell me if something changed underneath."
5 · Fix "So the first fix is to the eval: add the missing slices from production, repair the grader, pin what was moving. Then I fix the agent against the corrected suite."
6 · Prevent "And I keep them tied together: a weekly flow of production failures into the suite, sampled online scoring, and a check that offline and online metrics move together."
Close "Fixed means the suite fails when production fails."

stages.name: Symptom
stages.html:
"I write down both sides before theorising."

Offline Production
Regression suite near 100%, unchanged escalation rate rising
Capability suite flat user retries and rephrasing rising
Judge scores steady sampled online judge score falling, or corrections rising

An average can hide it: an 80% blended rate is consistent with most traffic at 90% and a new quarter of it at 50%.

stages.name: Hypotheses
stages.claim: the suite, the world, or the ground under both
stages.html:
"Six candidates, grouped by what moved."

Group Hypothesis
Production moved new intents, new customers, new document types, longer sessions
The suite stopped measuring saturated at 100%; tuned against for months; one-sided cases
The graders are lenient a judge that likes fluent answers; a check on the reply, not the state
Something changed underneath an unpinned model alias; a tool's API or data changed
Environment gap mocked tools behave better than real ones; clean data offline, messy data live
One trial per case the suite measures "can", production experiences "does every time"

stages.name: Evidence
stages.html:
"Two checks separate most of these."

Check 1:cluster recent production runs by intentmap each cluster to suite taskslist clusters with no task
Check 2:failing production tracesrun the offline graders on themdo they fail?
Observation Likely cause Next action
A large cluster has no suite tasks traffic drift; a stale suite add tasks from that cluster
Offline graders pass runs users rejected lenient or wrong grader re-calibrate against human labels
Model or tool version differs from the suite's run a silent change pin; re-run the suite on the live versions
Fails live, passes with mocked tools environment gap record real tool responses into the rig
Failures concentrate in long sessions suite cases are short add multi-turn cases
Same task passes offline, fails 1 in 3 live one trial per case several trials; report pass^k

stages.name: Root cause
stages.claim: usually a stale or lenient suite
stages.html:
"A worked example of how drift hides."

suite: old intents only                         → 90% and steady
production this month (illustrative):
  75% of traffic: old intents at 90%
  25% of traffic: a new intent at 50%
blended = 0.75 × 0.90 + 0.25 × 0.50 = 0.80     ← ten points below what the suite reports

Model or harness? Often neither changed. The measurement did not follow the traffic. Where the agent really is weaker on the new slice, the trajectory tells me if context or tools were missing (harness) or if it had everything and still failed (model).

stages.name: Fix
stages.claim: the eval first, then the agent
stages.html:
"Changing the agent against a suite that can't see the problem is guessing."

Order:add the missing slicesrepair or re-calibrate graderspin moving versionsconfirm the suite now failsfix the agentsuite passescanary
Repair Detail
Coverage 20–50 tasks from the uncovered clusters, drawn from real failing runs
Graders check final state; re-measure judge agreement on the new slice
Trials several per task
Environment recorded real tool responses; realistic, messy inputs

The step in bold is the proof: a corrected suite must go red on the current agent.

stages.name: Prevent
stages.claim: keep the suite tied to production
stages.html:
"Automated evals are one layer; the others exist to catch what they miss."

Layer Catches
Offline suite regressions before release
Production monitoring and sampled online scoring new failure types, drift
User feedback and corrections what users actually reject; corrections are labels
Transcript review subtle quality problems no metric names
Guard Practice
Coverage report share of production intent clusters with at least one task
Saturation watch a capability suite at 100% gets harder tasks
Correlation check when offline goes up, does the online metric follow?
Nightly run against pinned versions catches provider-side drift

My own goldens carry this caution in their header: provisional labels, consistent but not yet calibrated. A green run on them is not yet a claim about real interviews.

Fix layer: eval first; then prompt/context, tools or model as the trajectories indicate.

followUps.question: "The evals pass, so the complaints must be noise."
followUps.html:
Production is the ground truth about production.

Trusting the suite Checking the suite
Complaints dismissed complaints become tasks
The suite stays green and wrong the suite goes red, then gets fixed

followUps.question: 🧪 The new intent grows from 25% to 40% of traffic, at the same rates. What happens to blended quality?
followUps.html:
It falls to 74%, with no change to the agent or the suite.

0.60 × 0.90 + 0.40 × 0.50 = 0.54 + 0.20 = 0.74
suite still reports 0.90                      ← the gap is now 16 points

followUps.question: How do you detect drift before users complain?
followUps.html:
Watch the inputs, not only the outputs.

  • Intent mix over time, from clustering or a classifier.
  • Share of runs with no close match in the eval set.
  • Steps and tool mix per run: a shift suggests new task types.

followUps.question: Could the suite be over-fitted?
followUps.html:
Yes, if every prompt change for months was tuned against it.

Sign Control
Suite climbs, online metric doesn't a held-out set nobody tunes on
Fixes are case-specific rules rotate tasks in from production

followUps.question: Leadership asks, "can we trust the eval numbers?" What do you say?
followUps.html:
As far as they've been checked against production, and here's that check.

  • Report coverage and offline–online agreement alongside the pass rate.
  • Say what the suite doesn't cover.
  • Treat a disagreement as a finding, with an owner and a date.

dontSay: "The evals are green, so we're fine." — green on which traffic?
"Users are just being picky." — put their failing runs through the graders.
"We'll tune the prompt until the complaints stop." — fix the measurement first.
"Our suite has 500 cases." — how many look like this month's traffic?

agentic-ai-q56.testing: that you design the repository and its feedback loops for the agent (guides before, sensors after), bound what it can touch, and keep a person on the merge.
agentic-ai-q56.trap: "Give it the repo and a good system prompt", or a huge instructions file that tries to say everything.
agentic-ai-q56.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what tasks it takes: bug fixes, small features, migrations? Does it work with a developer or in the background? And how good are the tests, because they're its main feedback."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The limits are the context window, the cost of a run, and review capacity. The agent can write code faster than people can review it, so review is the real bottleneck."
3 · Baseline design "The harness has two halves. Guides steer before it writes: a short instructions file that points to deeper docs, the conventions, the task as a checkable spec. Sensors check after: type checks, linters, tests, structural rules, then a reviewer."
4 · Deep-dive "The hard part is making the checks fast, deterministic and readable by the agent. A failing test with a clear message is something it can fix on its own. A vague failure, or a ten-minute build, breaks the loop."
5 · Failure modes "It fails in known ways: marking work done without running it end to end, editing the tests to make them pass, large unreviewable diffs, and following instructions hidden in an issue or a dependency."
6 · Evolve "It evolves by turning every repeated review comment into a rule the tooling enforces, and by measuring merged changes per unit of review time, not lines written."
Close "The repository is the harness: what the agent can read steers it, and what CI checks keeps it honest."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Three answers size the whole design."

Question Changes
Which tasks: fixes, features, migrations, upgrades? how checkable "done" is
Paired with a developer, or background runs? permissions, sandbox, hand-off
How much of the code has fast, trustworthy tests? where the agent can be left alone
What may it touch: branch, CI, secrets, production? blast radius
Who reviews, and how much can they take? the real throughput limit

Earning the agent: a mechanical migration with a known recipe may be a script. The agent pays where the steps can't be listed in advance.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"The binding constraint is usually review time."

per task (illustrative): 25 steps × 12,000 tokens average context ≈ 300,000 input tokens, mostly cache reads
wall-clock: 25 model calls + test runs; a 30 s test suite run 5 times = 2.5 min of the run
review: 20 agent pull requests a day × 15 min each = 5 hours of reviewer time   ← the bottleneck
Limit Design response
Context window a short index file; deeper docs read on demand
Cost per task step and token budgets; stop with a partial result
Review capacity small diffs; machine checks before any person looks

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"Every control is either a guide or a sensor, and either deterministic or model-based."

Deterministic Model-based
Guide (before) repo layout, typed interfaces, an allowed-commands list instructions file, architecture docs, examples of good changes
Sensor (after) type checker, linter, tests, dependency-direction rules a reviewer agent, a person

The grid is Böckeler's (Apr 2026). The instructions file works as a table of contents: build and test commands, where things live, links to the rest.

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: make the feedback fast and legible
stages.html:
"An agent improves quickly against a failing test and not at all against its own confidence."

Property of a sensor Why the agent needs it
Fast (seconds, per change) it runs many times per task
Deterministic a flaky test teaches the wrong lesson
A message that says what to do "import from ui into domain is not allowed; move the type to shared" can be acted on
End to end where it matters unit tests and a curl miss failures a user would hit
Runnable by the agent one command to set up, one to test
Requirement In the instructions Enforced outside
Follow the layering rules described a structural test fails the build
Don't weaken tests stated test files protected or flagged in the diff; coverage can't drop
No secrets, no production stated sandbox with no credentials and restricted network
Small changes stated a diff-size limit in CI
Nothing merges unreviewed — branch protection: a person merges

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Each one has a control outside the model."

Failure Control
Declares done without running it "done" means the acceptance check passed in CI
Edits the test to make it pass flag test changes; a reviewer checks them first
A large, tangled diff one task, one small change; a size limit
Drift over a long task a task list with pass flags, a progress file, commits per step
Instructions hidden in an issue, a web page or a dependency treat all of it as data; no network or secrets in the sandbox
Runaway cost step, token and wall-clock budgets
Entropy: duplicated helpers, stale docs scheduled clean-up tasks, also checked by sensors

Blast radius: reading the repository is free, writing to a branch is reversible, merging and deploying are gated by a person.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"The harness improves where a fast, objective check can be added."

Loop:a review comment repeatswrite it as a lint or structural ruleCI enforces itthe comment never needs repeating
Measure Why
Merged changes per hour of review the real throughput
Share of runs passing all sensors first time harness quality
Reverts and incidents from agent changes the cost side
Task success on a private suite of past issues, pass^k the release gate for harness changes

On a model upgrade, I re-test which guides and resets still carry load. Evaluation hook: the private task suite. Fix layer: harness: repository, CI and permissions.

followUps.question: "Put everything the agent needs into one big instructions file."
followUps.html:
A long file crowds the context and goes stale; an index stays useful.

Encyclopedia Table of contents
Loaded on every task, mostly irrelevant short; deeper docs read when needed
Rules described rules enforced by tooling
Nobody knows what's outdated docs checked like code

followUps.question: 🧪 The test suite takes 10 minutes and the agent runs it 6 times per task. What does that do?
followUps.html:
It turns every task into an hour of waiting.

6 runs × 10 min = 60 min of test time per task
with a 30 s targeted suite: 6 × 0.5 = 3 min     ← the full suite runs once, in CI

Fast, targeted checks in the loop; the slow suite as the final gate.

followUps.question: How do you stop it changing the tests to get green?
followUps.html:
Make test changes visible and costly.

  • Flag any diff touching tests; review those first.
  • Coverage and assertion counts can't fall.
  • The acceptance check is written before the task starts, and the agent can't edit it.

followUps.question: Would you let it merge on its own?
followUps.html:
Only for classes of change where the sensors are a complete check.

Change Merge
Formatting, dependency bumps with full tests automatic, with rollback
Behaviour changes a person

followUps.question: How do you justify the harness work to a team that just wants the agent switched on?
followUps.html:
It's the same investment that helps people, and it compounds across models.

Investment Pays
Fast tests, clear errors, structural rules people and agents alike
A private task suite every future model and harness decision
Skipping it review becomes the bottleneck and trust falls

dontSay: "We wrote a detailed system prompt for it." — say what CI enforces.
"It writes thousands of lines a day." — measure merged, reviewed changes.
"The agent tests its own code." — with which sensor, and can it edit that sensor?
"It has access to everything a developer has." — it should have less.

spine: Why "valid token" is the wrong check
Residual risk and what I monitor
agentic-ai-q57.testing: whether you treat spend as part of authorisation and give agents their own narrow, budgeted identity, instead of a developer's master key.
agentic-ai-q57.trap: "Rotate the key and add a billing alert." The alert arrives after the money is gone.
agentic-ai-q57.spoken:
# · Beat Cue Say
1 · What budget is authorisation "The token was valid, so the fix isn't stronger authentication. Spend has to be part of authorisation, checked before every model call."
2 · Why agent loops spend fast "An agent loop can make thousands of calls overnight. Billing alerts arrive hours later, after the money is gone."
3 · How · actors human, CI, agent tokens "I'd give each actor type its own credential. Humans get short OIDC sessions, CI gets workload identity, and agents get delegated tokens scoped to tools and models."
4 · How · gate $/hour checked per call "The gateway checks the token's model allow-list and remaining dollar budget on every call. At the cap it returns 429 and pauses the run."
5 · How · anomaly velocity vs baseline "It also compares spend velocity with the token's normal rate, plus geography and time. Past three times baseline it throttles, downgrades or forces re-auth."
6 · How · lifecycle expiry, kill switch "Agent tokens expire quickly, rotate automatically and have a per-agent kill switch, and sub-agents share the parent's budget."
7 · Watch spend like logins "I watch spend per token like failed logins: velocity, model mix, output size, new networks. I migrate old keys in phases so integrations don't break."
Close loss capped by design "The goal is that a stolen token can cost at most one hour's cap, not a night's bill."

stages.name: The asset and the attacker
stages.claim: the asset is the spending power behind a token
stages.html:
What was stolen is a key that can call expensive models without limit, and an agent loop turns that into a bill in hours.

attacker loop: 1 call / 2 s × 3,600 s/h × 8 h      = 14,400 calls   (illustrative)
each call ≈ 30K input + 4K output tokens on a frontier model
spend scales with calls × tokens × price            ← nothing in the token limits any of the three
Attacker How they get the token
outsider leaked in a repo, a CI log, a client app
insider or a compromised agent reuses a broad key for work it wasn't meant to do

stages.name: The attack path
stages.html:
The token was genuine, so authentication passed; nothing asked who was using it, for what, or how fast it was spending.

Path:leaked keyauthenticated any model any volume billing alert next morning$140K

stages.name: Why "valid token" is the wrong check
stages.claim: one key type for three kinds of actor
stages.html:
A human, a CI pipeline and an autonomous agent behave differently, so they need different credentials and limits.

Actor Credential Expected behaviour Limit
human OIDC session, short-lived token, MFA interactive, bursty per-user quota
CI pipeline workload identity (OIDC federation), no static secret known environment, narrow scope per-pipeline scope
agent delegated agent token: tools, models, $/hour, expiry loops, can spend fast budget enforced per call, kill switch

The agent's token is a sandboxed worker identity, never a copy of the developer's key.

stages.name: Layered controls
stages.claim: budget checks before the model call, not billing alerts after
stages.html:
The gateway checks actor, scope and remaining budget on every call, and pauses the run when the budget is gone.

Prove it — a budget in the authorisation path:

TOKENS = {"agt-42": {"actor": "agent", "models": {"small"}, "usd_per_hour": 20, "baseline_usd_h": 4}}
spent = {}
def authorize(tok, model, est_usd, hour):
    t = TOKENS.get(tok)
    if t is None: return "401 unknown token"
    if model not in t["models"]: return f"403 model '{model}' not allowed for {t['actor']}"
    used = spent.get((tok, hour), 0) + est_usd
    if used > t["usd_per_hour"]: return f"429 budget: ${used:.0f} > ${t['usd_per_hour']}/h, run paused"
    spent[(tok, hour)] = used
    return "ALERT anomaly" if used > 3 * t["baseline_usd_h"] else "200 ok"
print(authorize("agt-42", "frontier", 0.5, 2))                 # stolen token tries the big model
results = [authorize("agt-42", "small", 0.9, 2) for _ in range(30)]  # overnight loop, 30 calls in an hour
print(results[12], "|", results[13], "|", results[22], "| allowed:", results.count("200 ok") + results.count("ALERT anomaly"))
# → 403 model 'frontier' not allowed for agent
# → 200 ok | ALERT anomaly | 429 budget: $21 > $20/h, run paused | allowed: 22

Run on Python 3. The loop is stopped at the hour's cap ($19.80 spent), and the anomaly alert fires when spend passes three times the token's normal rate.

Layer Control
identity actor type, owner, project, environment carried in the token
scope allowed models, tools, projects; no privilege escalation
budget $/hour and $/day per token, checked before the call
anomaly spend velocity vs the token's baseline, new geography, odd hours → throttle, downgrade, re-auth
lifecycle short expiry, rotation, per-agent kill switch

stages.name: Residual risk and what I monitor
stages.claim: spend velocity is a security signal
stages.html:
A thief can still spend up to the cap, so caps are sized to the damage I can accept, and spend is watched like logins.

Monitor Alert when
$/hour per token vs baseline > 3× baseline
model mix per token a small-model token asks for frontier models
output tokens per call sudden jump (exfiltration or loops)
calls from new networks or regions first seen
tokens with no expiry any exist

Migration matters too: issue scoped tokens alongside old keys, warn, then enforce, so existing integrations don't all break on one day.

followUps.question: Isn't a billing alert enough?
followUps.html:
No. Billing is reported after usage; inference spend happens in minutes.

Alert:spendbilling pipeline (hours)alerthumanrevoke
Gate:each callbudget check429 at the cap

followUps.question: How do you size the cap without breaking real agents?
followUps.html:
From each agent's observed spend: cap at a few times its normal peak, with a request path for more.

cap = p99 hourly spend × headroom     ← e.g. $6/h × 3 = $18/h  (illustrative)

followUps.question: Why not give CI a static API key in its secrets?
followUps.html:
Static secrets leak through logs and forks; workload identity issues a short-lived token only to that pipeline, at run time.

Static key Workload identity
Lifetime until rotated minutes
Usable elsewhere yes, if leaked no, bound to the workload

followUps.question: An agent spawns sub-agents. Whose budget do they spend?
followUps.html:
The parent run's budget, split down the delegation chain, never a fresh budget per child.

Delegation:run budget $20child A gets $8child B gets $8parent keeps $4any child over → paused

followUps.question: You have 400,000 integrations on old keys. How do you migrate?
followUps.html:
In phases: observe, warn, enforce, with the riskiest keys first.

Phase Action
observe tag every key's actor, owner and normal spend
warn soft caps that alert, deprecation notices
enforce hard caps on agent and unattended keys first, then the rest

dontSay: "The token was valid, so the request was fine" — validity isn't authorisation for unlimited spend.
"We'll set up a billing alert" — it fires after the money is gone.
"Agents use the developer's key" — an agent needs its own narrow, budgeted identity.
"Rotate keys every 90 days" — a stolen key spends its damage in one night.

agentic-ai-q58.testing: whether you can split an agent's work into fixed-option gates and open-ended generation, and keep the threshold in code.
agentic-ai-q58.trap: "Replace the LLM with the faster, cheaper model," or "a confidence of 0.9 means it's right."
agentic-ai-q58.spoken:
# · Beat Cue Say
1 · What gates vs generation "I'd use a decision model for the agent's fixed-option gates, and keep the LLM for anything it has to write or reason through."
2 · Why many small decisions "An agent makes many small decisions per run, like routing, policy checks and is this done. On a frontier LLM each one costs seconds and returns text to parse."
3 · How · decision model probabilities, one call "A decision model like Jev returns probabilities over options I define. Several questions run in parallel in about a hundred milliseconds."
4 · How · thresholds bands in code "My code turns confidence into bands: act automatically, confirm, or send to a human. Approval still gates anything irreversible."
5 · How · LLM plan, args, replies "Planning, tool arguments and replies stay on the LLM, because a decision model writes no text."
6 · Watch labelled set per version "I set thresholds on labelled examples and re-check them on every model version, because valid labels can still be wrong."
Close split by step "So in practice it's both, split by step: a decision model for the small gates, and the LLM for the real work."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: does the step have a fixed set of answers?
stages.html:
The axis is the shape of the output: a choice among options I define, or words and arguments the model must write.

A decision model (TypeSafe's Jev, Sep 2026; OpenAI's Decisions API, GA Oct 2026) takes state and typed questions and returns probabilities: a choice, a yes/no noul, or a score, with a confidence. It writes no text and calls no tools.

Agent step Output shape Fits
route to a sub-agent one of N names decision model
"does this need approval?" yes/no decision model
"did the tool answer it?" yes/no decision model
plan the next steps free text LLM
fill tool arguments structured, open values LLM
reply to the user free text LLM

stages.name: Where a decision model wins
stages.claim: many small gates, fast and calibrated
stages.html:
On fixed-option gates it is faster, always parseable and gives a probability I can threshold.

Prove it — choice confidence and bands (Jev's documented formula):

def confidence(probs):                       # choice: (p_max - 1/n) / (1 - 1/n)
    n, p = len(probs), max(probs.values())
    return (p - 1 / n) / (1 - 1 / n)

def gate(probs, auto=0.8, floor=0.5):
    c = confidence(probs)
    label = max(probs, key=probs.get)
    return f"{label}: {c:.2f} -> " + ("auto" if c >= auto else "confirm" if c >= floor else "human")

print(gate({"billing": 0.90, "technical": 0.07, "other": 0.03}))
print(gate({"billing": 0.62, "technical": 0.30, "other": 0.08}))
# → billing: 0.85 -> auto
# → billing: 0.43 -> human

Run on Python 3. All questions in one request run in parallel on the same state, in about 100 ms (vendor-quoted, as of Oct 2026), so five gates cost about one call.

stages.name: Where the LLM wins
stages.claim: anything that must be written or reasoned
stages.html:
Planning, tool arguments, explanations and replies need generation, which a decision model doesn't do.

Need Decision model LLM
free text or code
reasoning across several facts split into narrow questions
arithmetic, counting, dates do in code better in code too
labels that change per call define per request
an explanation for the audit log

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: can I write the options down and test a threshold?
stages.html: If I can list the answers and label a few hundred examples, the gate goes to a decision model; if not, it stays on the LLM.

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
In a support agent I'd move triage, refund intent and policy checks to a decision model, and keep planning and replies on the LLM.

Run:ticketdecision model: team? refund? risky? (one request)bands in codeLLM plans + calls toolsLLM repliesapproval gate before money moves

Thresholds live in code, are tied to a pinned model version, and are re-checked on every upgrade.

followUps.question: The output is always a valid label. Doesn't that make it reliable?
followUps.html:
No. Valid isn't right; it removes parse errors, not wrong judgements.

Removes Doesn't remove
malformed JSON, retries a confident wrong label
free-text parsing a vague question's blended answer

followUps.question: Why is confidence lower than the top probability?
followUps.html:
Confidence measures how far the top probability is above an even split.

confidence = (p_max − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n)
           = (0.62 − 0.333) / (1 − 0.333) ≈ 0.43     ← 3 options

followUps.question: The vendor ships a new version. What breaks?
followUps.html:
Your thresholds: probabilities shift between versions, so a 0.8 cut-off can mean a different error rate.

Upgrade:pin versionreplay labelled set on the new onere-fit thresholdsmove the pin

followUps.question: Can a decision model be your guardrail?
followUps.html:
It can be the detector, not the enforcement.

  • Detector: noul "asks to bypass policy?" → probability.
  • Enforcement: code blocks the tool call or asks a human.

followUps.question: Is it worth adding another vendor for this?
followUps.html:
Only if gates are a large share of your LLM calls or latency; measure that first.

Measure first Why
share of calls that are fixed-option gates the size of the win
p95 latency spent in gates the user-visible win
accuracy per band on labelled data the risk

dontSay: "Replace the LLM with Jev" — it doesn't write text or call tools.
"0.9 confidence means 90% right" — only after you check it on labelled data.
"One question: is this a good, safe, on-policy reply?" — split it into narrow questions.
"Thresholds are set once" — they move with every model version.

agentic-ai-q59.testing: whether you can turn "summarise" into a graph with typed state, a reducer for parallel writes, and a stop condition, live, in a few minutes.
agentic-ai-q59.trap: one node that sends the whole document to the model, or a "refine until good" loop with no bound.
agentic-ai-q59.spoken:
# · Beat Cue Say
1 · What map-reduce graph "I'd write a map-reduce graph: split the document, summarise chunks in parallel, join them, and shrink once if it's still too long."
2 · Why too big for one call "A long document doesn't fit one prompt, and parallel chunks cut latency. The round cap stops a refine loop from running forever."
3 · How · state reducer on summaries "State is a TypedDict, and summaries has an operator.add reducer so parallel map nodes append instead of colliding."
4 · How · fan-out Send per chunk "A conditional edge from START returns one Send per chunk, so each chunk runs the map node in parallel."
5 · How · stop check, shrink, END "The reduce node joins and counts rounds. A check routes to END when it's short enough or the cap is hit, otherwise one shrink step."
6 · Watch fake model, assert state "I test with a fake model and assert on state: fan-out count, the reducer and the cap. Then a small faithfulness eval with the real model."
Close a bounded workflow "It's a bounded workflow, not an agent: the path is in code, and only the summaries come from the model."

stages.name: Read the task
stages.claim: ask the size, the target length and the failure budget
stages.html:
Before typing, I'd ask three things, because they pick the graph.

Ask Changes
Does the document fit one context window? single call vs map-reduce
Target length or format the stop check
Latency and cost budget parallel map, round cap, model per step

Assume it doesn't fit, so I'll split it.

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.claim: map-reduce with a bounded shrink step
stages.html: Split into chunks, summarise each in parallel, join, and shrink only if it's still too long, at most a fixed number of rounds.

stages.name: Write it
stages.claim: typed state, a reducer, Send for the fan-out
stages.html:
The reducer on summaries is what lets parallel map nodes write without overwriting each other.

# langgraph 1.2.16, as of Oct 2026; summarise() stands in for an LLM call
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import Send

def summarise(text: str) -> str:                      # fake LLM: keep the first sentence
    return text.split(". ")[0].rstrip(".") + "."

class State(TypedDict):
    doc: str
    max_words: int
    summaries: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]     # reducer: parallel writes are appended
    final: str
    rounds: int

def fan_out(s: State):                                 # one Send per chunk → map in parallel
    chunks = [p for p in s["doc"].split("\n\n") if p.strip()]
    return [Send("map", {"chunk": c}) for c in chunks]

def map_node(s: dict): return {"summaries": [summarise(s["chunk"])]}
def reduce_node(s: State):
    joined = " ".join(s["summaries"])
    return {"final": joined, "rounds": s.get("rounds", 0) + 1}
def check(s: State):                                    # bounded: stop when short enough or after 2 rounds
    return END if len(s["final"].split()) <= s["max_words"] or s["rounds"] >= 2 else "shrink"
def shrink(s: State): return {"final": summarise(s["final"])}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("map", map_node); g.add_node("reduce", reduce_node); g.add_node("shrink", shrink)
g.add_conditional_edges(START, fan_out, ["map"])
g.add_edge("map", "reduce")
g.add_conditional_edges("reduce", check, ["shrink", END])
g.add_edge("shrink", END)
app = g.compile()

doc = ("Refunds are issued within 5 days. Card refunds may take longer.\n\n"
       "Orders ship in 48 hours. Remote areas take a week.\n\n"
       "Returns need the original box. Opened items are inspected.")
out = app.invoke({"doc": doc, "max_words": 20, "summaries": [], "final": "", "rounds": 0})
print(out["summaries"])
print(out["final"], "| rounds:", out["rounds"])
short = app.invoke({"doc": doc, "max_words": 8, "summaries": [], "final": "", "rounds": 0})
print(short["final"], "| rounds:", short["rounds"])
# → ['Refunds are issued within 5 days.', 'Orders ship in 48 hours.', 'Returns need the original box.']
# → Refunds are issued within 5 days. Orders ship in 48 hours. Returns need the original box. | rounds: 1
# → Refunds are issued within 5 days. | rounds: 1

Run with uv run --with langgraph==1.2.16, offline. In the interview, summarise becomes model.invoke(prompt).

stages.name: Trace it
stages.html:
Three chunks fan out, three summaries append through the reducer, and the check routes to END or to one shrink.

Step Node Writes State after
1 START → 3 × map one summary each, in parallel summaries = 3 items (appended)
2 reduce final = joined, rounds = 1 17 words
3a check (max 20) → END done
3b check (max 8) → shrink → END "Refunds are issued within 5 days."

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.html:
Each follow-up changes one part of the graph; the state and reducer stay.

They ask Change
"Keep the summary faithful" add a check node: every claim must appear in a chunk
"It must survive a crash" compile with a checkpointer, pass a thread_id
"Let a human approve it" interrupt() before END
"Chunks have headings" split on headings, carry the heading into each summary
"Drop the reducer" parallel writes to one key raise InvalidUpdateError

stages.name: How it performs
stages.claim: map calls dominate, rounds are capped
stages.html:
Cost is roughly one call per chunk plus one or two reduce calls, and latency is one map round in parallel.

calls ≈ chunks + reduce + shrink rounds   = 3 + 0 + ≤1          (summarise is the only model call)
latency ≈ slowest map call + shrink       ← map runs in parallel
cap: rounds ≤ 2                           ← the loop can't run away

followUps.question: Why not send the whole document in one call?
followUps.html:
If it fits, do that; the graph is for documents larger than the window, or when you need parallelism.

Document Pick
fits comfortably one call
larger than the window map-reduce

followUps.question: What does Annotated[list, operator.add] do here?
followUps.html:
It's the reducer: writes from parallel map nodes are concatenated instead of the last one winning.

Without:3 parallel writes to summariesInvalidUpdateError
With:3 writes[s1] + [s2] + [s3]

followUps.question: How do you stop a "refine until good" loop running forever?
followUps.html:
A round counter in state and a check that ends the run at the cap, whatever the quality.

  • State: rounds: int, incremented by the node that loops.
  • Check: rounds >= cap → END, with the best summary so far.

followUps.question: Is this an agent or a workflow?
followUps.html:
A workflow: the path is fixed in code, and only the summaries come from the model.

This graph An agent
Who picks the next step code the model
Loops bounded by a counter until the model stops

followUps.question: How would you test it?
followUps.html:
Swap the model for a fake, as above, and assert on state; then a small eval for faithfulness.

Test Asserts
unit, fake model fan-out count, reducer order, the cap
eval, real model every summary claim is supported by its chunk

dontSay: "I'll loop until the summary is good" — say what stops it.
"Parallel nodes just write the list" — without a reducer they collide.
"It's an agent" — the path is fixed; call it a workflow.
"Summarise the whole doc in one prompt" — not when it doesn't fit.
